details.d: Priests recorded Nile flood heights on the quay about 2,900 to 2,700 years ago. Ask your guide to show you.
High in the First Pylon's doorway, names and dates of nineteenth-century visitors, carved when sand filled the court.
The alabaster block at the foot of Taharqa's column is where the god's boat was set down.
The giant columns are stacks of half-drums. Look for the joints.
Eleven columns in the northern half fell in 1899 and were rebuilt by 1902. Look for cleaner blocks and slight misalignments.
On the south outer wall, a plastered-over Kadesh battle shows under later wars. Best in raking light.
Rows of small holes near the sanctuary held pegs for gold sheeting. The holy core was gilded.
Faded painted saints on the Festival Hall columns, from its time as a church.
The Festival Hall columns swell towards the top, like wooden tent poles.
By the lake, the top of her second obelisk lies on its side: carving made to be seen from thirty metres below, now at eye level.

qa.q: Why was the First Pylon never finished?
qa.a: It is usually dated to Nectanebo I, of the last native dynasty, about 2,350 years ago. The Persians reconquered Egypt in 343 BC, and the later Ptolemies spent their building money on temples such as Edfu and Philae. The ramp shows the work simply stopped.

qa.q: How did they stand a 300-tonne obelisk up?
qa.a: Nobody wrote it down. The unfinished obelisk at Aswan shows the quarrying, with hard dolerite pounders. Barges carried them on the flood; a relief at Hatshepsut's temple shows two obelisks on one boat. For raising, the leading theories are earth and brick ramps, then tipping the stone into a sand-filled pit and letting the sand out slowly.

qa.q: Did Thutmose III hate Hatshepsut?
qa.a: Probably not as the story is often told. They shared the throne for about twenty years, and attacks on her images began late in his reign, roughly twenty years after her death. The common view today is political: making his son's succession look clean. Walling her obelisks hid them, but he did not topple them.

qa.q: Where are Karnak's other obelisks?
qa.a: Several left in antiquity. The Lateran obelisk in Rome, the tallest ancient obelisk standing anywhere, was begun at Karnak by Thutmose III and finished by Thutmose IV; the Romans took it in the fourth century AD. The obelisk of Theodosius in Istanbul is another of Thutmose III's from Karnak. The Paris obelisk comes from Luxor Temple.

qa.q: Could ordinary people come in?
qa.a: Mostly not. The inner temple was for priests and the king. People saw the god's boat at festivals and prayed at the outer walls. At the east end of the precinct, Ramesses II built a chapel for the god who hears prayers, where people could bring requests without entering.

qa.q: What was the Cachette?
qa.a: From 1903 Georges Legrain dug a court south of the Hypostyle Hall and found a pit packed with statues: about 800 in stone and some 17,000 bronzes. Priests buried them in antiquity, probably in Ptolemaic times, to clear space while keeping sacred objects inside the temple.

qa.q: Is Karnak lined up with the winter solstice?
qa.a: Possibly. The main axis points to about 116 degrees, close to the midwinter sunrise, and the Franco-Egyptian team argues the alignment was deliberate. Other researchers doubt it and point to the river and older buildings. Still debated.

qa.q: What did the priests do all day?
qa.a: Each morning priests purified themselves in the Sacred Lake, opened the shrine, woke the god's statue with hymns, washed, dressed and fed it. The food was then shared among the temple staff. Karnak also ran land, herds and workshops, and employed thousands at its height.

practical: Plan 2 to 2.5 hours: about ninety minutes with me, then thirty alone.
Shade only in the Hypostyle Hall and some side halls. The Great Court and the lake are open sun.
At least a litre of water each. Hats, sunscreen, closed shoes: floors are uneven.
Toilets are normally at the visitor centre by the entrance. Go before you start.
Cruise groups crowd the site from about eight to eleven; the hall thins out around midday.
Guards may offer roped areas or poses for a tip. You may decline; never cross ropes.
The Open Air Museum usually needs its own ticket: check on the day.
Sound and Light is optional in your programme, in French. The boat sails to Esna on Day 5, so check which evening it fits.

kids.d: Count the rams that still have a king between their paws, one row each. Closest guess wins the first seat on the coach.
Hold hands and see how many of you it takes to circle a giant column. Then work out how many of your tallest family member, stacked, reach the top at 21 metres.
Find raised relief in the north half of the hall and sunk relief in the south half. Explain the difference without touching the wall.
In the Botanical Garden, draw one plant or bird. At dinner, the others guess what it is.
Teenagers: did Thutmose III wall in Hatshepsut's obelisk to hide her or to keep it? One minute per side.

glossary.d: King of the gods, the hidden one, fused with the sun. Karnak is his house.
A monumental gate of two sloping towers.
A hall whose roof rests on columns.
High windows above a lower roof that light the middle of a hall.
Thutmose III's Festival Hall, 'Splendid of Monuments'.
Small blocks from Akhenaten's buildings, reused as fill.
The morning sun as a scarab beetle.

tonight: If you could take one object home from Karnak, which one?
Thutmose III or Hatshepsut: who comes out better from what we saw?
Ramesses II carved his name on other kings' work. Stealing or recycling?

sites.name: Edfu, the Temple of Horus
sites.kicker: Day 6 morning · by horse carriage from the boat
sites.hook: The best-preserved temple in Egypt, and the clearest textbook of how a temple works.

story.title: Hathor comes to visit
story.text: Every year, in high summer, a statue of the goddess Hathor was lifted onto a boat at her temple at Dendera, north of Luxor, and carried upriver to Edfu, a journey of days. There she met the god Horus, and they were married again in a festival called the Beautiful Meeting. Crowds lined the river and the temple walls carry the stories. The temple itself was buried in sand and houses until the 1860s, when it was dug out. Because of that, it is nearly complete.

steps: Horse-carriage ride from the quay to the temple
The granite falcons and the great pylon
The open court with columns on three sides
The first hall of columns (hypostyle)
Second hall, the offering hall, the sanctuary
The sanctuary: the granite shrine
The walkway round the outside: Horus against Set (ask)

dont_miss.d: A granite falcon in a crown stands at the gate. The god protecting the entrance.
A giant king grabbing his enemies by the hair. It is a symbolic picture, repeated on every pylon, and it keeps order.
As you walk inwards, the floor rises, the ceiling lowers and the light fades. That is by design.
In the sanctuary a polished stone shrine is much older than the temple. It was reused from the earlier building.

dont_miss.t: The walls are full of text
dont_miss.d: Edfu has more hieroglyphic text than almost any other temple: festival rules, building records, a list of the temple library.

easy: Look at the faces on the reliefs: many have been chiselled off by early Christians, who lived in and around the temple.
The ceilings in some halls are black from old cooking fires.
Look for the tall grooves in the pylon. Flagpoles with banners were set in them.
Small rooms off the main halls were storerooms, a treasury and even a 'library' of papyrus scrolls.
The Ptolemies were Greek kings. Notice how they dress as pharaohs on the walls.
ask: How do we read the sequence of rooms, and where would the priests have walked?
Why were the Ptolemies, who were Greek, building a temple in this style?
Can we see the walkway around the outside with the scenes of Horus and Set?
How did the temple stay so complete?
What is the Beautiful Meeting?
quests: Look closer
Find a scene where the king gives something to a god. What is he holding, and what is the god holding?
Estimate
The pylon is about 36 m high. If a floor is 3 m, how many floors? Compare it with a building near home.
tips: The carriage ride is part of the experience. A small tip for the driver is normal. Ask the guide what is usual.
Early morning is quieter. The stone is cool and the light enters the court from the side.
Temple interiors are dim. Phone torches are handy, but do not shine them on painted ceilings.

deep.guide_line: One complete temple in one morning: from the sunlit gate to the dark granite shrine, then round the back to watch Horus harpoon a very small hippo.

briefing.intro: Edfu is the one temple in Egypt where nothing important is missing: the roof is on, the doorways are intact, and the side rooms still have their purpose carved over the door. So this is where we stop reading about temples and walk through one. A horse carriage takes us from the river through the town. We come out in front of a gateway thirty-six metres high that faces south. Behind it the temple runs in a straight line northwards: an open court, two halls of columns, smaller rooms, and the sanctuary at the far end, ringed by chapels. Around the whole building runs an open stone corridor between the temple and its high outer wall. We go in along the axis, come back through the corridor, and then I leave you about forty minutes on your own. Keep one idea in mind: this was a house for a god and a machine for keeping the world in order. Every carving had a job.

know.d: Most temples run east to west. Edfu runs south to north, gateway at the south, sanctuary at the north. The earlier temple here ran east to west. The compass matters for the visit: in the morning the sun comes from the south-east, lighting the gateway at an angle and the west corridor wall head-on.

Work began on 23 August 237 BC under Ptolemy III. The gateway decoration was finished in 57 BC under Ptolemy XII, father of the famous Cleopatra. About 180 years, interrupted by revolts in the south. The founding date is carved on the walls, which is why we know it to the day.

The Ptolemies descended from one of Alexander the Great's generals and spoke Greek at court. On these walls they wear the crowns and kilts of kings two thousand years older. Paying for traditional temples kept the powerful priesthood on their side.

Sand and silt filled the temple to about twelve metres and a village grew on top. Napoleon's scholars saw only the tops of the gateway in 1798. Auguste Mariette began clearing it in 1860. The burial saved the roof, and the people living in it blackened some ceilings with soot.

Edfu carries more hieroglyphic text than almost any temple: hymns, festival rules, offering lists, room sizes in cubits, a library catalogue, even recipes. It fills fourteen published volumes and translation is still going on. Ask your guide to read you one label.

Edfu's ancient name was Behdet, and its god Horus of Behdet. You will meet him as a falcon, as a falcon-headed man, and as the winged sun disc over every doorway. The Greeks matched him with Apollo and called the town Apollinopolis Magna.

Many faces and hands were hacked off. People who lived here after Egypt became Christian saw the images as alive and dangerous, and disabled the parts that made them work. Notice how low figures suffered more than high ones: they could be reached.

numbers: about 1.5 h, including about 40 min on your own

tour.title: The carriage ride and the first view
tour.where: From the quay, horse carriages wait on the riverside road. The ride runs inland through town for roughly ten to fifteen minutes.
tour.look: This is the only working-town street you will see up close on the cruise, so look out, not at your phone: bakeries with round flat bread cooling on racks, sugar cane stacked outside juice stalls, donkey carts, schoolchildren in uniform. The temple appears suddenly at the end of a street, below you. The modern town stands on centuries of rubble, metres above the temple floor. Whichever way the path from the ticket area leads you, aim for the gateway: it is the south front.
tour.story: The carriages, called hantour, have done this run for well over a century and feed many families in town. Drivers usually hope for a tip on top of the fare already paid, sometimes more than once. Agree the amount with your guide before you climb in, pay it once at the end of the return ride, and decline further requests kindly. Six of you need two carriages: one adult in each. If a horse looks lame or thin, tell your guide; visitor complaints do reach the welfare groups working with the drivers.
spot: Sugar cane at the juice stalls
The first glimpse of the gateway over the rooftops
tour.photo: Film ten seconds with the horse's ears at the bottom of the frame. Both hands on the phone, the road is bumpy.

tour.title: The Birth House
tour.where: In the forecourt, in front of the gateway on its west side (on your left as you face the gateway). The small temple with columns round its outside.
tour.look: This is the mammisi, the birth house. Walk round its outside. On the square blocks above the column capitals, find Bes, the squat, bearded, tongue-out god who protected mothers and newborns. Inside, goddesses nurse a divine child, and the ram-headed god Khnum shapes the baby on a potter's wheel. Most of it was decorated under Ptolemy VIII, a century before the gateway.
tour.story: At Edfu, Horus and Hathor of Dendera were a couple with a son, Harsomtus, 'Horus who unites the Two Lands'. His birth was re-enacted here every year. The point was also political: the king claimed to be that divine child, so the celebration renewed his right to rule. Birth houses are a late idea; you will see others at Kom Ombo and Philae. This is one of the best preserved.
tour.ask: Which scene shows the birth itself, and who are the goddesses helping?

tour.title: The gateway and its falcons
tour.where: Stand in the middle of the forecourt, about forty metres back, facing north towards the doorway between the two towers.
tour.look: Two sloping towers, a doorway that once held cedar doors, and on each tower a giant Ptolemy XII holding enemies by the hair and raising a mace while Horus and Hathor watch. Above, rows of offering scenes. The four tall grooves held flagpoles with coloured pennants; the square holes above them held the clamps. Granite falcons guard the doorway. The towers are hollow, with stairs and rooms inside, normally closed.
tour.story: The two towers stood for the two mountains of the horizon with the sun rising between them, so the gateway is a picture of sunrise. The smiting scene is the oldest image of kingship in Egypt, used for some three thousand years. It records no particular battle. It says: chaos stays outside, order lives inside. In the morning the sun comes from the south-east, on your right, and rakes across the carving. That is the best moment to read it.
spot: The tiny captives under the raised arm
tour.photo: Step back until the full height fits at 0.5x, family on the lower third, a little to one side of the doorway.

tour.title: The court of offerings
tour.where: Walk through the gateway into the open court, columns on three sides, the hall facade straight ahead to the north.
tour.look: Thirty-two columns run round the east, west and south sides. Compare neighbours: palm, papyrus, lotus and mixed bouquets, no two side by side the same. Turn round to see the inside of the gateway, with the doorways to its stairs. Low on the court walls run long processions, boats included. On festival days this court was full of townspeople; it was probably as far as most of them came.
tour.story: Here the festival of the Beautiful Meeting ended. Each summer Hathor's statue sailed upstream from Dendera and stayed about two weeks. The texts list bread, beer, cattle and geese, and describe a happy, drunk town. Ask your guide to find Hathor's boat on the walls. The court was also where offerings were piled on altars in the open air, in full view of the sun. Then count the hacked faces at eye level against those higher up.
spot: Capitals that do not match their neighbours
tour.photo: In the morning the east colonnade is in shade: line the family up inside it, facing west, sunlit court behind.

tour.title: The crowned falcon, the library and the first hall
tour.where: North end of the court, at the doorway into the first hall of columns. The library is the tiny room just inside it.
tour.look: The famous granite falcon wears the double crown, the white crown of the south set inside the red crown of the north. On the low screen walls of the facade, two gods pour water over the king, the stream drawn as a chain of ankh signs. Inside, the small library has a list of its book titles carved on the wall. In the hall, twelve columns, a soot-stained ceiling, and walls where the king founds the temple: stretching the cord with the goddess Seshat, moulding a brick, presenting the finished building to Horus.
tour.story: The falcon is Horus and also the king, since every living king was 'the Horus'. Nobody went further without being purified, and the priests here shaved their bodies, washed several times a day and wore only linen. The library list names rituals, protective spells and temple knowledge; the scrolls are gone, the catalogue remains. The foundation scenes are a promise in pictures: this house was built by the right person, to the gods' plan.
spot: Water as a chain of ankh signs
The book list in the library
tour.ask: Can you read us one title from the library list?

tour.title: Laboratory, offering hall and the roof stairs
tour.where: Continue north into the second, darker hall, then the narrower offering hall. Side doors open into small rooms; stairways open east and west.
tour.look: Off the second hall, find the laboratory: a small room covered floor to ceiling in neat columns of recipes for temple perfumes, oils and incense, including kyphi. Other doors led to storerooms, and on the east a passage towards the Nilometer stairs. In the offering hall, look at the two stairways: carved priests carry the god's shrine up one side and down the other, tilted to match the slope of the steps.
tour.story: Temples were also workshops and estates with fields, cattle and accounts. The recipes give quantities and cooking times over days; attempts to recreate kyphi differ, because some ingredients are hard to identify. At New Year, in high summer, priests carried Horus up to the roof to meet the sun and be recharged by its light, some in falcon and jackal masks. Your feet follow theirs.
spot: Priests in animal masks on the stair walls
A door labelled with what it stored
tour.ask: Which kyphi ingredients can scholars identify for sure?

tour.title: The sanctuary and the ring of chapels
tour.where: Straight ahead on the axis, the last doorway. A narrow corridor runs round the sanctuary with chapels opening off it.
tour.look: In the middle stands a shrine cut from one block of polished dark granite, about four metres high with a pyramid top, carved for Nectanebo II, one of the last native kings, in the 4th century BC. The Ptolemies built their new temple around it. In front, a modern replica of the god's processional boat. Then walk the corridor: nine or ten chapels for gods linked to Horus, including Min, Osiris, Khonsu, Hathor and Ra, with traces of blue paint on some ceilings.
tour.story: The statue of Horus, probably small and gilded, lived inside that shrine. Every dawn the high priest broke the clay seal, sang the god awake, washed, dressed and fed him, and sealed him in again at night. Keeping an older king's shrine was a statement: the Greek dynasty presented itself as heir of the Egyptian one. The chapels show gods working in families, never alone. The corridor is the quietest spot when groups crowd the sanctuary.
spot: Bolt holes for the shrine doors
Blue paint on a chapel ceiling
tour.photo: No flash. Brace the phone on the doorframe, tap on the shrine to expose, barque in the foreground.

tour.title: The outer corridor: Horus, Set and the Nilometer
tour.where: Leave through a side door into the open corridor. Walk the west side first, then round the north end and down the east side.
tour.look: A canyon of stone more than twelve metres high. On the inner face of the west wall, Horus stands in a boat and spears Set as a hippopotamus, so small it would fit under a table. Count the harpoons. High on the temple side, lion-headed waterspouts drained the roof. On the east side, a stairway goes down under the outer wall towards a well: the Nilometer. It may be gated; you can usually look down.
tour.story: The myth and the sacred play are in episode l04. Here, notice the method: the god huge and calm, the enemy tiny. Many scholars think a full-size dangerous animal in stone could itself be dangerous, so it was shrunk and speared. The Nilometer well rose and fell with the river, so priests read the flood without leaving the temple. A high flood meant good harvests and higher taxes, and temples were landowners too.
spot: The hippo the size of a dog
The steps down to the Nilometer
tour.photo: Shoot along the corridor, with one person walking away from you for scale.

alone.intro: I leave you in the court for about forty minutes. The temple is one long rectangle with one way in, so nobody gets lost. Pick a plan, keep the younger ones in sight in the dark rooms, and drink before you start.

plans.d: Walk the axis again in silence: court, first hall, second hall, offering hall, sanctuary. At each doorway notice the step up and the darker room. Then go out to the west corridor and count the harpoons properly. Finish at the crowned falcon for the portrait you could not take with the crowd.

The full circuit for teenagers: west corridor, the north end behind the sanctuary, the east side down to the Nilometer stairs, back into the temple for the laboratory and the stair processions, and out to the Birth House to find Bes.

The inner rooms keep the night's cool. Sit in the corridor round the sanctuary and play the capital game: each person sketches one column capital in five lines and the others find it later in the court. Cross the sunny court last, on the way out.

alone.meet: Meet at the crowned falcon at the time your guide gives, with a phone alarm five minutes before. The carriages do not wait long.

photos.where: Middle of the forecourt, about 40 m south of the gateway, camera facing north.
photos.when: Early to mid morning, sun in the south-east.
photos.how: 0.5x at chest height so the towers lean less. Family off-centre on the lower third. Ask your guide, or prop the phone on a bag with the timer.
photos.avoid: The queue at the doorway. Wait for a group to pass through.

photos.where: North end of the court, beside the falcon in the double crown.
photos.when: Morning, face lit from the side.
photos.how: Crouch to the falcon's chest height so the crown stands against the dark doorway. One person beside it, not touching. Portrait mode, tap to expose on the face.
photos.avoid: Leaning on the statue; guards will stop you.

photos.where: Inside the east colonnade of the court, looking west.
photos.when: Morning, while the east side is shaded.
photos.how: Subject in shade, sunlit columns behind. Tap on the face and let the background go bright.
photos.avoid: The sunny strip: hard shadows under the eyes.

photos.where: North-east corner of the court, looking south-west to the inside of the gateway.
photos.when: Before 10 am.
photos.how: 0.5x, phone low, the row of different capitals leading to the gateway.
photos.avoid: The sun in frame once it clears the gateway.

photos.where: West corridor, inner face of the enclosure wall.
photos.when: Morning, sun raking from the east.
photos.how: Fill the frame with Horus, harpoon and hippo, then a second shot with a hand pointing for scale.
photos.avoid: Flat midday light that erases the carving.

photos.where: Sanctuary doorway, on the axis.
photos.when: Just after a group leaves.
photos.how: Phone braced on the doorframe, no flash, exposure pulled down a touch. Night mode if you hold still.
photos.avoid: Flash, and torches on paint.

photos.where: In the carriage on the way back.
photos.when: Late morning.
photos.how: Front camera at 0.5x, horse's ears and the street in frame.
photos.avoid: Shooting while the carriage turns in traffic.

details.d: Many small rooms have their use carved above the doorway: library, laboratory, storerooms. A temple with signage.
Above each flagpole groove on the gateway, square holes held the timber clamps that kept the poles upright.
The goddess of measuring wears a seven-pointed star on a stick on her head. Find her laying out the temple with the king.
Lion heads stick out high on the outer temple walls. Rain from the flat roof left through their mouths, guarded on the way out.
On the stair walls, priests carrying the god climb at exactly the angle of the steps.
Some priests have animal heads. Scholars think they wore masks; a real Egyptian pottery jackal mask survives in a museum in Germany.
Look high up for names and dates scratched by nineteenth-century visitors, who stood on the sand at the old ground level.
The black ceilings are soot from later fires. At Esna, restorers cleaned similar soot and found bright original paint underneath.
The walls give room sizes in cubits, about 52 cm each. Pace out a doorway and compare.
Over almost every doorway spreads a sun disc with wings and two cobras: Horus of Behdet guarding the door.

qa.q: Why does Edfu face south?
qa.a: Nobody knows for sure. The earlier temple ran east to west, and its gateway may have been left standing at a right angle to the new one. Orientation could be decided by older buildings, the space available in the town, or links with other sacred sites. Ask your guide which explanation he prefers.

qa.q: Did the Greek kings believe in Egyptian gods?
qa.a: Partly, probably. The Ptolemies kept Greek gods at court in Alexandria but paid for Egyptian temples and took Egyptian titles; some were crowned in Memphis. Whatever they believed, the priesthood was a major landowner and a voice of the countryside. Supporting it mattered, especially after revolts in the south in the 2nd century BC, which interrupted the work at Edfu for years.

qa.q: How do we know the exact start date?
qa.a: The building inscription on the walls gives it: day 7 of the third month of the summer season, year 10 of Ptolemy III, which scholars convert to 23 August 237 BC. It then dates each stage, including when the doors were hung, which makes Edfu one of the best-dated buildings of the ancient world.

qa.q: Were the walls painted?
qa.a: Yes, in strong colours: blue and green for hieroglyphs, red-brown skin for men, yellow for women, dark blue ceilings with yellow stars. Little paint survives at Edfu except on some ceilings and in protected corners. Recent cleaning at Esna and Dendera has shown how bright these temples were.

qa.q: Who was allowed inside?
qa.a: Ordinary people reached the forecourt, and the court on festival days. The halls were for priests, the sanctuary for the high priest and, in theory, the king. The public met the god when his statue came out in procession, which is also when oracles were given.

qa.q: Why are only some faces destroyed?
qa.a: The attackers aimed at what made an image work: faces, eyes, hands, feet. Many scholars link it to Christian communities of the 4th to 7th centuries AD, though some damage may come from later villagers living in the temple. High figures were out of reach and survive better.

qa.q: Where did the stone come from?
qa.a: The sandstone came from Gebel el-Silsila, about 40 km upriver, where the Nile runs between sandstone cliffs. You may pass it this afternoon. Blocks were cut there, loaded on barges and floated downstream with the current, and quarrymen left their marks and prayers on the cliffs. The granite shrine came from Aswan, further south.

qa.q: Is anything still unexplained?
qa.a: Plenty. Scholars still debate how the festival texts relate to what was actually performed, how the Horus and Set play was staged, and how real the library list was. The full translation of Edfu's texts is a long-running German-led project. Enjoy the local stories your guide tells, and ask which ones come from the walls.

practical: About 1.5 hours on site plus about 30 minutes of carriage rides.
Early is best: several boats arrive together and the court fills after about 9 am.
Hat, sunscreen and water. Shade only along the colonnades.
Dim rooms and raised thresholds: proper shoes and a hand on the younger ones.
No flash; torches off painted ceilings. Check the current photo rules on the day.
Toilets are near the entrance area, none inside the temple.
Hawkers wait at the carriage stand and the exit. A polite no and walking on works.
Shoulders and knees covered: respectful, and good sun protection.

kids.d: Count every falcon: statues, carvings, winged sun discs, falcon-headed gods. Over 30 is a good score; the winner picks the next photo spot.
In the west corridor, find the smallest hippo and count its harpoons. Then explain to your parents why it is so small.
From court to sanctuary, count the steps up at each doorway. Does the floor really rise?
Teenagers: explain in two minutes a day in the temple, from breaking the seal at dawn to sealing the shrine at night.
Photograph one hacked face and one intact face in the same scene. At dinner, everyone guesses why one was spared.
Should the horse carriages become electric carts? Two reasons for, two against, then vote.

glossary.d: The great gateway with two sloping towers.
A hall whose roof rests on many columns. Say 'HY-po-style'.
Birth house, a small temple for the god's child. Say 'MAM-ee-see'.
Ancient name of Edfu. Say 'BEH-det'.
Child of Horus and Hathor. Say 'har-SOM-tus'.
Native king of the 4th century BC, owner of the granite shrine. Say 'nek-ta-NEE-bo'.
Temple incense whose recipe is carved in the laboratory. Say 'KEE-fee'.
Horse-drawn carriage. Say 'han-TOOR'.

tonight: If you could carve one label over your bedroom door, what would it say?
The hippo was carved tiny so it could not hurt anyone. Which modern pictures do people still treat as if they had power?
The Ptolemies dressed as pharaohs to be accepted. Clever politics, or a kind of lie?

sites.name: Kom Ombo
sites.kicker: Day 6 afternoon · on a bend of the river
sites.hook: A temple with twin doors: one half for a crocodile god and one half for a falcon god.
facts: from about 180 BC, under the Ptolemies

story.title: Two gods, one roof
story.text: Most temples serve one god. This one has two of everything: two entrances, two halls, two sanctuaries, side by side. The northern half belongs to Haroeris, a form of the falcon god Horus, and the southern half to Sobek, the crocodile god of the river. The temple sits on a bend of the Nile where sandbanks were once covered in basking crocodiles. Sobek was feared and honoured. Mummified crocodiles were left here as offerings.

steps: Arrive at the temple on its bluff above the river
The courtyard and the double entrance
The two halls of columns
The two sanctuaries at the back
The walls on the outside: the medical instruments
The Crocodile Museum, if included (ask)

dont_miss.d: North and south halves mirror each other. Walk both and compare.
A man with a crocodile's head, receiving offerings. Look for the crocodile on a shrine.
A relief on the back wall, in the corridor behind the temple shows what look like medical tools: a lancet, a sponge, forceps. Historians are careful about what exactly it shows.
Texts on the wall list the festivals of the year.
The temple is placed to catch the river bend. Turn round and look at the Nile.

easy: Look for a round stone well with a stair: it is the Nilometer, used to measure the flood.
Crocodile mummies of all sizes were found nearby. The Crocodile Museum next door shows some.
The columns have capitals shaped like papyrus and lotus. Notice how the colours remain on a few.
A small chapel of Hathor was used to store crocodile mummies.
ask: Why two gods in one temple?
How do we know which half is which?
What does the medical relief really show?
How did people look after and mummify crocodiles?
Did Sobek protect people from crocodiles or did people fear him?
quests: Look closer
Find a mirrored pair of scenes, one on each side of the temple. What small differences can you spot?
Debate
A crocodile god and a falcon god sharing a temple: who is likely to have been more popular with farmers, and why?
tips: A short stop at a lovely time of day. The temple can be crowded by cruise groups, so move along the walls.
The Crocodile Museum is a separate building. Your programme does not list it, so ask.

deep.guide_line: A temple cut in two down the middle: we walk the falcon's half and the crocodile's half, find the surgeon's toolkit, then watch the sun go down over the river from the Nilometer.

briefing.intro: Kom Ombo is short, beautiful and best at the end of the day. The temple stands on a low mound right above the river, so close that the boat almost moors at its feet. Its front faces south-west, towards the water, and in the late afternoon the low sun lights the columns straight on and turns the sandstone gold. The building is a double temple. An invisible line runs down the middle from the front door to the back wall, and everything is doubled on either side: two doorways, two aisles through the halls, two sanctuaries. Facing the temple from the court, the left half belongs to Haroeris, Horus the Elder, the falcon, and the right half to Sobek, the crocodile. We walk in along one axis, look at the back wall, come out along the other, and finish at the Nilometer as the sun sets. Then you have time on your own, and the Crocodile Museum is the obvious last stop after dark.

know.d: The temple's long axis runs from south-west, at the river, to north-east. The double doorway faces the water, so the facade gets the evening sun. The Nilometer and the Crocodile Museum are on the north-west side, towards the left as you face the temple. The old Birth House is at the south-west corner, near the river.

Each god has a household. Sobek lives with Hathor and their son Khonsu. Haroeris lives with a goddess called Tasenetnofret, 'the good sister', and their son Panebtawy, 'lord of the Two Lands'. Scenes for the two families mirror each other across the axis.

An older temple stood here in the New Kingdom, but almost nothing remains. Ptolemy VI began the present building around 180 BC; later Ptolemies, including Ptolemy XII, added halls and decoration. Roman emperors, among them Augustus and Tiberius, finished the court and enclosure, shown on the walls as pharaohs.

The front of the building, including most of the gateway, was lost to the river, to earthquakes and to people taking ready-cut stone. The French engineer Jacques de Morgan cleared and restored the site in 1893. What survives is the inner part, which is why you see column stumps in the court and roofless halls.

The bend of the river below once had sandbanks where crocodiles basked. Nile crocodiles grow over five metres and kill people. They disappeared from Egypt north of the High Dam in the 20th century; today they survive in Lake Nasser. Sobek was honoured in places where the danger was daily.
The ancient name was Nubt, 'gold', perhaps because of gold routes from the eastern desert. The Greeks wrote it Ombos. 'Kom' is Arabic for a mound, which is what the buried temple was for centuries.

The plain around Kom Ombo is one of Egypt's big sugar cane areas, with a large sugar factory. In the 1960s, thousands of Nubian families displaced by Lake Nasser were resettled in new villages on this plain. You may hear Nubian spoken around the site.

numbers: from about 180 BC, Roman additions after
Crocodile mummies found in the area
about 1 h with the guide, plus free time and the museum

tour.title: Arriving from the quay
tour.where: From the boat, walk up from the riverside to the entrance area. Stop where you first see the whole temple on its mound, the river behind you.
tour.look: Notice how high the temple sits. The mound is centuries of rubble and silt, and the river is right below. The columns you see first are the front of the halls; the gateway in front of them has mostly gone. To your left, on the north-west side, is the modern building of the Crocodile Museum. Look at the colour of the stone now, and again in an hour: sandstone changes from pale yellow to orange as the sun drops behind the west bank.
tour.story: Nineteenth-century travellers drew this temple from the water, half buried, with the river eating at its edge. Part of the forecourt and the Birth House were carried off by floods before the river was controlled, and the modern stone embankment below you now protects the rest. The setting has not changed: a temple built to look after a bend of the river and the creatures in it.
spot: The temple on its mound from below
The museum building to the north-west
Your boat among the others at the quay
tour.photo: Turn round once at the top of the slope: the river with the boats moored below makes a good wide shot in this light.

tour.title: The court and the double doorway
tour.where: Enter the court in front of the halls. Stand on the axis, at the altar base in the middle, facing north-east towards the facade.
tour.look: The court of the emperor Tiberius had sixteen columns on three sides; you see their lower parts, some with paint still bright on the drums. In the centre is the base of an altar, with small basins for offerings to each god. Ahead, the facade of the first hall has two doorways side by side, each under its own winged sun disc. That is the whole temple in one look: the left door leads to Haroeris, the right to Sobek.
tour.story: Columns usually come with a story about plants: here the capitals mix papyrus, symbol of Lower Egypt, and lotus or sedge, symbol of Upper Egypt. The court was the public part of the temple, where people gathered on festival days. Tiberius, who ruled from Rome and never came here, is shown making offerings as an Egyptian king. Rome kept the system running because it worked: the temples were landowners and centres of local life.
spot: The altar basins, one for each god
tour.photo: From just behind the altar, frame both doorways symmetrically. The low sun lights the facade straight on.

tour.title: The first hall: two aisles, one roof
tour.where: Step up into the first hall of columns through either doorway. Stand between the two central aisles.
tour.look: Look up. On the ceiling over the two central aisles, flying vultures with spread wings, the goddesses Nekhbet and Wadjet, in blue. On the columns, colours survive better than almost anywhere on the cruise. On the facade walls inside, the king is purified by gods pouring water, Horus on one side and Thoth on the other, and crowned by the two goddesses of Upper and Lower Egypt. Find Sobek with his crocodile head and Haroeris with his falcon head on the walls of their own halves.
tour.story: A purification scene stands at the threshold of almost every temple: no one entered the god's house unwashed, not even the king in a picture. The flying vultures guard the processional route, which is why they run along the axes. Inlaid eyes once filled the eye sockets of some figures here; none survive. Look at the hands as well: hands and faces were the parts later visitors attacked, because they made an image act.
spot: Water drawn as a stream of ankh signs
tour.photo: Phone flat on your palm, pointed straight up at the vulture ceiling, 0.5x.

tour.title: The second hall and the calendar
tour.where: Continue through the twin doorways into the second, smaller hall, then the narrow transverse rooms beyond, each a step higher.
tour.look: In this second hall the reliefs list festivals and sacred places. In the narrow rooms beyond, look for the calendar: rows of small, regular signs, one entry per day, with the months and the festivals of the year. Your guide will point out the season signs. Nearby, the king and the goddess Seshat lay out the temple. Each room is smaller, darker and higher than the last.
tour.story: The Egyptian year had three seasons of four months: flood, growing and harvest, each month thirty days, plus five extra days at the end. The calendar told priests which offerings and processions were due on which day, a duty roster in stone. The extra five days were the birthdays of Osiris, Horus the Elder, Set, Isis and Nephthys, so Haroeris here had his own birthday among them. Scholars still use these temple calendars to work out the religious year.
spot: The day-by-day rows of the calendar
tour.ask: Can you show us today's date on the calendar, roughly?

tour.title: The two sanctuaries and the hidden passage
tour.where: At the back of the inner temple, two doorways side by side. Left: Haroeris. Right: Sobek.
tour.look: Little remains of the sanctuaries above floor level: you see the bases where the shrines and boats stood. Look between the two rooms. In the thickness of the wall runs a narrow hidden passage, and below the floor are crypts. Many guides say a priest hid here and spoke as the god's voice. On the walls nearby, look for the gods of both families receiving offerings.
tour.story: An oracle priest in the wall is a lovely story and possible, but nobody can prove how the passage was used. It may simply have been a secure corridor or storage. What is certain is that the gods answered questions in Egypt, usually when their statues were carried out in procession: the boat dipped or moved to show yes or no. Ask your guide what he thinks, and notice that the two sanctuaries are exactly the same size. Neither god outranks the other.
spot: The hidden passage between the sanctuaries
tour.ask: Which god was more popular with local people, Sobek or Haroeris?

tour.title: The back wall: the surgeon's toolkit
tour.where: Leave the inner temple and walk round into the corridor at the back, between the temple and its enclosure wall. The relief is on the inner face of the rear wall.
tour.look: A seated god faces a row of objects laid out like a display: blades, hooks, forceps, a saw, sponges, scales, small pots. Nearby, look for seated figures on what are often described as birthing chairs. This is the most argued-over carving at Kom Ombo. It dates from the Roman period. Episode s09 tells the debate; here, take time to look and decide which objects you can name.
tour.story: Kom Ombo was a place people came to hoping for healing, so reading this as a surgeon's kit makes sense, and Egyptian medical papyri describe operations, splints and wound care. Other scholars think some objects are tools for ritual, for opening the mouth of a statue or measuring offerings. Both may be partly right: in Egypt, medicine and ritual overlapped. The back of the temple, closest to the gods but reachable from outside the inner rooms, was where people without access to the sanctuary could address them.
spot: The seated figures on birthing chairs
tour.photo: Shoot at a slight angle so the side light gives the carving relief. A finger pointing at the forceps makes a good detail.

tour.title: The Nilometer and the river at sunset
tour.where: On the north-west side of the court, in front of the temple and to the left as you face it. A round well with a staircase spiralling down.
tour.look: Look down the well: a stone staircase winds down its inside to the water level far below. Next to it is a smaller basin. Some guides say young sacred crocodiles were kept there; that is possible, but not proven. Then walk to the edge of the terrace and look west: the river, its sandbanks and islands, palms on the far bank, and the sun dropping behind the desert hills.
tour.story: The well filled with groundwater that rose and fell with the river. In summer, priests read the height of the flood on marks along the stair. A good flood meant full granaries and higher taxes, a poor one meant hunger. Before the High Dam the river at this bend changed every year, depositing sandbanks where crocodiles basked. The temple was placed to watch over exactly this stretch of water, and this is the view it was built to face.
spot: The spiral steps inside the well
Sandbanks and islands in the river
tour.photo: For silhouettes, put the family on the terrace edge against the sunset, tap on the sky to expose, and ask everyone to stand apart so the shapes read.

tour.title: The Crocodile Museum
tour.where: The modern building on the north-west side, near the entrance path. Normally a separate visit; check with your guide whether it is included.
tour.look: A dark, cool room with crocodile mummies in glass cases, from about two metres to about four point three metres long. Look for the small ones, the embryos, the teeth, and statues of Sobek in different sizes. A model shows how the animals were buried in pottery coffins in a cemetery nearby. Some mummies still show their wrappings.
tour.story: Crocodiles were raised, kept and mummified as offerings to Sobek, hundreds of them, from hatchlings to giants. Scans of crocodile mummies elsewhere show that some were animals that died naturally, others were killed young, and some bundles hold only parts or even reeds. Pilgrims likely paid for a mummy as a gift to the god, a little like lighting a candle. The museum opened in 2012 and is one of the few in Egypt devoted to one animal.
spot: A baby crocodile in its wrapping
A Sobek statue with a sun disc crown
tour.photo: Glass reflects: put the phone lens against the glass at an angle and shade it with your hand. Check the photo rules at the door.

alone.intro: I leave you on the court for about thirty minutes. The temple is small, the light is changing fast, and the best things to do now are look again and take the evening photos. Keep the younger ones away from the edge of the terrace and the Nilometer.

plans.d: Go straight to the river terrace by the Nilometer and watch the sun go down. Take the silhouette shot and one wide shot of the river. Then walk back past the facade, which will have turned orange, and photograph the double doorway from the altar.

Walk the temple again alone, this time in through the right-hand door and up Sobek's aisle, then across to Haroeris's side. Look for one scene that differs between the two halves. Then the back wall for the instruments, out to the terrace for sunset, and the museum last, because it is lit and indoors.

plans.t: If you have more time after dark
plans.d: The temple is floodlit after sunset and looks completely different: the reliefs stand out in strong shadow. Walk the court with the lights on, then the museum. Night mode, phone braced on a column base.

alone.meet: Meet at the entrance to the museum at the time your guide gives. After dark, keep a phone torch on for the walk down to the quay.

photos.t: Family in the court, golden facade
photos.where: In the court, between the altar base and the facade, camera facing north-east.
photos.when: The last hour before sunset.
photos.how: Family on the column stumps or standing between two of them, the double doorway behind. The sun is low and in their faces, so ask them to turn slightly to one side and look at the camera only for the shot.
photos.avoid: Shooting into the sun from the other side; the family turns into black shapes.

photos.where: The terrace edge by the Nilometer, camera facing west over the river.
photos.when: From the moment the sun touches the hills to five minutes after.
photos.how: Everyone standing apart, side-on, arms or profiles visible. Tap on the sky to expose, then lower the exposure a little.
photos.avoid: A boat's mast cutting through someone's head; move a step.

photos.where: A Sobek relief in the halls or on the outer walls, ask your guide for a well-lit one.
photos.when: Late afternoon side light.
photos.how: One person stands beside the relief and copies the pose: one foot forward, staff in hand. Portrait mode at 2x.
photos.avoid: Touching the relief.

photos.where: On the axis, behind the altar, facing the facade.
photos.when: Late afternoon.
photos.how: Phone level, 0.5x, both doorways equally in frame. Use the grid lines.
photos.avoid: Groups in one doorway only; wait for balance.

photos.where: Central aisles of the first hall.
photos.when: Any time before dark.
photos.how: Phone flat on your palm pointing up, 0.5x, no zoom.
photos.avoid: Blown highlights where the roof is open; include only the roofed part.

photos.where: The sun deck of the boat, as you arrive or leave.
photos.when: Arrival in late afternoon, or the floodlit temple after dark.
photos.how: 2x zoom, horizon level, the temple on the right third with the river in front.
photos.avoid: Railings and deck chairs in the frame.

photos.where: In the court after dark.
photos.when: After sunset, once the floodlights are on.
photos.how: Night mode, phone braced on a column base. A family member holds a still pose for three seconds between two columns.
photos.avoid: Other visitors walking through the long exposure.

details.d: Above the facade, two separate winged sun discs, one over each doorway. Even the protection is doubled.
The lower column drums in the court still show blue, red and yellow paint, two thousand years old.
Columns by the hall entrance show lotus for the south and papyrus for the north. Find one of each.
Graffiti game boards have been reported scratched into the paving in the back parts of the temple. Ask your guide; bored priests or later visitors, nobody knows.
Some figures once had inlaid eyes of other materials. You can sometimes see the hollows.
Near the back of the temple, some scenes are only sketched or half carved, showing how sculptors worked from outline to finished relief.
Cartouches of Roman emperors sit next to pharaonic crowns. Ask your guide to read one emperor's name.
Look for the five extra days at the end of the year, the birthdays of the gods.
Between rooms at the back, a stairwell once led to the roof for ceremonies, as at Edfu.

At the south-west corner by the river, a ruined Birth House; near the lone gateway of Ptolemy XII, a one-room Roman chapel of Hathor, Sobek's wife here, where crocodile mummies were once stored and shown.

qa.q: Why two gods in one temple?
qa.a: No text explains it. Both gods were worshipped in this area long before the Ptolemies, and rebuilding for both, side by side, avoided choosing one community over the other. Horus the Elder was a god of kingship and the sky, Sobek of the river, fertility and raw strength. Together they covered most of what mattered on this bend of the Nile.

qa.q: Did people worship Sobek to be protected from crocodiles?
qa.a: Probably both protection and respect. Sobek could be fearsome, but he was also linked with the flood and fertility, and sometimes merged with the sun god as Sobek-Ra. Honouring the most dangerous animal in your daily life was a way to bring it inside the order of the world. Spells against crocodiles were also common.

qa.q: How do we know which half is whose?
qa.a: The inscriptions and the figures. Each half's doorways, walls and sanctuary carry the name and image of its god, and the families are named. The left half, facing the temple, is Haroeris; the right half is Sobek. Many guides call them north and south halves.

qa.q: Is the medical relief really surgical tools?
qa.a: Opinions differ. Many objects look like surgical tools, and Egyptian medical papyri show real knowledge of wounds and fractures. Some scholars argue the scene shows ritual instruments, and that it may be later than people think. The careful answer is that it shows a set of instruments presented to a god, and that some of them were probably used on bodies.

qa.q: Why did crocodiles disappear from here?
qa.a: Hunting over centuries, the growth of towns and farming along the banks, and finally the High Dam, which cut the river below Aswan off from the crocodiles of the south. Today Nile crocodiles live in Lake Nasser, behind the dam, and occasionally appear in the news when one is seen in the river.

qa.q: How were the crocodiles mummified?
qa.a: Like other sacred animals: dried with natron, coated in resin, wrapped in linen, sometimes with small crocodiles bundled together. Some were buried in pottery coffins in animal cemeteries. Scans show variety: whole animals, juveniles, parts and sometimes dummy bundles.

qa.q: Who were the Nubians resettled here?
qa.a: When Lake Nasser filled in the 1960s, it flooded Egyptian Nubia, south of Aswan. Around 100,000 people in Egypt and Sudan were moved. Many Egyptian Nubian families were resettled in new villages on the Kom Ombo plain. Some still speak Nubian languages, and many feel the loss of their old villages deeply.

qa.q: What happened to the front of the temple?
qa.a: The river shifted and floods undercut the bank, earthquakes shook the walls, and later builders took the dressed stones. The gateway and much of the court disappeared this way. De Morgan's clearing in the 1890s and later embankments protected what was left.

practical: Plan about 1 hour with the guide and about 30 minutes alone; the museum adds 15 to 20 minutes.
The visit is usually late afternoon or early evening. Ask when the boat arrives and what time the sun sets on the day.
It is a short walk from the quay, but there are steps and uneven paving. Torches help after dark.
Cruise groups arrive together and crowd the halls. Visit the back wall first or last to avoid them.
Little shade, but the sun is low by then. Hats still useful, sunglasses essential at sunset.
Toilets are near the entrance area.
Market stalls line the path from the quay. A polite no and walking on works.
Check photo rules for the museum at the door.
Mosquitoes can appear at dusk by the river: repellent for the younger ones.

kids.d: Find two scenes, one in each half, that mirror each other. List three small differences.
Count every crocodile you find: on walls, on statues, in the museum. Mummies count double.
At the back wall, name as many instruments as you can. Which would a modern surgeon recognise?
Which god would you pray to if you were a fisherman: the falcon or the crocodile? Defend it in one minute at dinner.
Take the same photo of the facade three times, twenty minutes apart. Watch the colour change.
Teenagers: explain how the Nilometer measured the flood without anyone going to the river.

glossary.d: Crocodile god of the river and its strength. Say 'SO-bek'.
Horus the Elder, the falcon god of this temple's left half. Say 'har-oh-EH-ris'.
'The good sister', wife of Haroeris here. Say 'ta-se-net-NOF-ret'.
'Lord of the Two Lands', son of Haroeris. Say 'pa-neb-TA-wee'.
Moon god, here the son of Sobek and Hathor. Say 'KON-soo'.
Ancient name of Kom Ombo, meaning 'gold'. Say 'noobt'.
Arabic for a mound.
A well or stair for measuring the river's level.

tonight: If you could build a temple for two gods today, which two would share it, and how would you split the rooms?
Should the crocodile mummies be on display, or reburied? Why?
What would you measure every day if you were a priest at a Nilometer today?

sites.name: Aswan: High Dam, felucca and Elephantine
sites.hook: The place where the Nile was stopped, and one of the loveliest river views in Egypt.
facts: High Dam about 45 min, felucca about 1 h
built 1960 to 1970, about 3.8 km long, 111 m high

story.title: The lake that moved two temples
story.text: For thousands of years, the Nile rose every summer and fell every autumn. In 1970, the High Dam ended that. It stored the water in a lake nearly 500 km long, gave Egypt power and protected it against drought and flood. But the lake covered Nubia, a region with its own language, villages and temples. Around 100,000 people were moved and a worldwide appeal helped to save the temples, including Philae and Abu Simbel. You will see one of them tomorrow.

steps: High Dam: a viewpoint over the lake and the dam wall
The Lotus monument beside the dam
Philae temple (next page)
Felucca on the Nile around Elephantine
Elephantine: look for the Nilometer and old town

dont_miss.d: Nearly four kilometres of rock and earth. On one side, a lake. On the other, the old river.
A wooden sailing boat with a triangle sail. The captain uses wind and current, as people have here for thousands of years.
Named 'elephant' either from the ivory trade or from the shape of the granite boulders in the river.
Dark granite boulders in the river mark the First Cataract, the old southern border of Egypt.

easy: Granite here is the stone of obelisks. Look at the pink and black rocks on the shore.
The Nubian houses on the west bank are painted in bright colours.
Look for the Nilometer steps on Elephantine, used to measure the river's height.
Birdwatchers love this stretch. Look for egrets on the rocks.
ask: What did the dam give Egypt, and what did it take away?
Where did the Nubians go, and what do they say about it today?
How did the flood work before the dam?
What does the captain do to sail against the wind?
quests: Look closer
Find rock that is not sandstone. What colour is it? Where have you seen it earlier in the trip?
Estimate
The dam is about 3.8 km long. How long would it take to walk across at a normal pace?
tips: On the felucca, sit as the captain asks. Sunscreen and a hat are needed because there is no shade.
Swimming from the boat is not recommended. Keep phones on lanyards or in bags.

deep.guide_line: A day of granite and water: you stand on the wall that stopped the Nile, then sail the old frontier as the sun goes down.

briefing.intro: Aswan is where Egypt used to end. South of here the Nile breaks over a field of dark granite boulders, the First Cataract, and for most of ancient history that was the border with Nubia. The town on Elephantine Island grew rich on ivory, gold and stone. Today has two halves. In the morning you see the modern answer to the river: the High Dam, a wall of rock and clay nearly four kilometres long that ended the yearly flood in 1970. Philae comes in between and has its own page. Later you see the old answer: a felucca, a wooden boat with one triangular sail, moving the way boats have moved here for thousands of years. I will show you what to look at on the dam, how to read the rocks and islands from the water, and where to sit for the best sunset photograph of the trip.

know.d: A cataract is a stretch of rapids where hard granite breaks through the softer sandstone. Boats could not pass easily, so the First Cataract became a natural frontier. Egypt counted its cataracts from north to south: the first is here, the sixth is north of Khartoum. The dams have tamed the rapids, but the boulders are still in the river around you.

The British built the first Aswan dam from 1898 to 1902 and raised it twice. It drowned Philae for most of each year. The High Dam, about six or seven kilometres upstream, followed from 1960 to 1970 with Soviet engineers and credit. The old dam still works, and your coach will probably cross or pass it on the way.

Water stored for dry years, two or three harvests a year instead of one, protection against killer floods, and twelve turbines that once supplied about half of Egypt's electricity. In the drought of the 1980s, the stored water kept Egypt farming.

The flood stopped, so the black silt that fed the fields for five thousand years now settles in the lake. Farmers buy fertiliser, the Delta coast erodes, and some fields grow salty. Behind the wall, the lake drowned Lower Nubia: about 100,000 to 120,000 people were moved in Egypt and Sudan.

Aswan granite is pink, grey and black and keeps a polish for thousands of years. It went into obelisks, sarcophagi and colossal statues all the way down the river. The granite you saw at Giza and in Cairo began its journey on these banks.

The island in front of modern Aswan was the ancient town, called Abu, meaning elephant: maybe for the ivory trade, maybe for the grey boulders that look like bathing elephants. It held temples to Khnum, the ram god of the cataract, and to the goddess Satet, and a famous Nilometer.

An open wooden sailing boat with one triangular sail on a long sloping yard. The north wind carries it south, the current carries it north, and the captain zigzags when he must. There is no engine. When the wind drops you drift, and that is part of the charm.

numbers: about 43 million cubic metres, roughly sixteen Great Pyramids
about 500 km long, about 5,250 square km
about 6:10 pm (Egypt is still on summer time); check your phone

tour.title: The High Dam, facing the lake
tour.where: At the viewpoint on top of the dam, walk to the parapet on the side of the wide still water. You are facing south, towards Sudan.
tour.look: In front of you is Lake Nasser, so wide that on a hazy day the far shore disappears. It runs about 500 kilometres south; its Sudanese end is called Lake Nubia. Notice the shores: bare rock and sand, almost no green. Look down at the slope below you: the dam is a mountain of rock and sand with a clay core. On the western shore, look for a small sandstone temple: Kalabsha, moved there in the early 1960s.
tour.story: Under that water lies Lower Nubia: villages with painted domes, palm groves and more than twenty temples. UNESCO launched an appeal in 1960 and dozens of countries sent money and archaeologists. Some temples were moved around the lake. Some were given away as thanks: the Temple of Dendur is now in the Metropolitan Museum in New York, Debod in a park in Madrid, Taffeh in Leiden, Ellesyia in Turin. The people had fewer choices: Egyptian Nubians were moved to new villages near Kom Ombo.
spot: Kalabsha temple on the western shore
The rock slope of the dam face
Power lines striding into the desert
tour.photo: Panorama mode from the parapet, phone level, from the lake round to the dam road.
tour.ask: Which Nubian temples were saved, and which are still under the lake?

tour.title: The High Dam, facing the river
tour.where: Cross the road to the northern parapet, above the narrow river. You are facing north, back towards Aswan.
tour.look: Now the contrast. On this side the Nile is a thin channel at the foot of the dam, tens of metres below the lake behind you. That drop is the whole point: water falls through tunnels on the east side to the power station, the long building near the river with power lines leaving it. Look west along the dam for a tall white tower shaped like an opening lotus: the monument to Soviet and Egyptian friendship, finished in 1971, about seventy metres high.
tour.story: The dam was a Cold War story. Egypt first asked the United States and Britain to fund it. In 1956 they withdrew, and President Nasser nationalised the Suez Canal to pay for the dam, which led to the Suez crisis. The Soviet Union stepped in. Work began in January 1960, and in May 1964 Nasser and the Soviet leader Khrushchev watched the river being diverted. The dam was completed in July 1970, a few months before Nasser died.
spot: The lotus monument to the west
tour.photo: Zoom 2x on the lotus tower with power lines in front: a 1960s picture of the future.

tour.title: Boarding the felucca
tour.where: At the quay on the east bank, facing Elephantine Island. Your felucca waits with others along the river front.
tour.look: Before you sit, look at the boat. The hull is wide and flat, so it can sail in shallow water between rocks. The mast is short; the long yard carrying the sail is much longer and slopes up towards the back. That is a lateen rig, used across the Mediterranean and the Red Sea. The cushions along the sides are your seats, and the captain decides who sits where: weight matters on a small boat.
tour.story: Here the wind blows mostly from the north and the current flows north. Going south, the captain raises the sail and lets the wind push. Coming back north, the current helps and he tacks: the sail swings across and the boat zigzags. The ancient Egyptians wrote 'to travel south' with a boat under sail and 'to travel north' with a boat with its sail down. You are about to feel that sign in your own body.
spot: The captain's rope at the stern

tour.title: The granite of the cataract
tour.where: Minutes after leaving the quay, as the boat passes the southern half of Elephantine. Look at the rocks to the south and west.
tour.look: These rounded boulders are granite, polished by the river and stained dark on top by a mineral crust. Some look like sleeping animals, and you may decide some look like elephants. This rock is far older than the sandstone of Edfu and Kom Ombo. Look for faint squared panels on the boulders at the edge of Elephantine: travellers, officials and quarrymen carved their names and prayers here for thousands of years.
tour.story: The rapids made Aswan a frontier and a toll gate. Every boat going south had to be hauled through or unloaded. Old Kingdom kings cut a channel through the rocks near the island of Sehel, a little further south. The quarries on the east bank, now inside the town, produced the obelisks of Karnak and the sarcophagi of the Valley of the Kings.

tour.title: Elephantine and the Nilometer
tour.where: As the boat runs along the east side of Elephantine. Near the southern end, look for a stone stairway going down into the water.
tour.look: That stairway is the Nilometer of the temple of Satet: steps running down to the river in a narrow corridor, with scales of numbers on the walls added over many centuries. Above it, look for mud-brick walls and the stone remains of the temples of Khnum and Satet, excavated by German and Swiss teams. The building near the southern tip is the Aswan Museum. The whole southern half of the island is a layered ancient town.
tour.story: Why measure the river here? Because Elephantine was the first place in Egypt the flood reached. Priests read the level on the steps and sent the news north: a low Nile meant hunger, a very high one broke dykes, a good one meant a rich harvest and higher taxes. This Nilometer was rebuilt in Roman times and used into the nineteenth century.
spot: The museum near the southern tip
tour.ask: Which scripts are on the Nilometer scale, and how high did the flood climb on it?

tour.title: The west bank hills and the Tombs of the Nobles
tour.where: As the boat turns into the western channel. The green island is Kitchener's Island; the high sandy hill on the west bank is Qubbet el-Hawa.
tour.look: Kitchener's Island is a botanical garden of palms and tropical trees. Then look up at the west bank: a steep hill of golden sand and rock with a small domed shrine of a local holy man on top. Below it, rows of dark doorways cut into the cliff, with sloping ramps up to them: the Tombs of the Nobles, the governors of Elephantine. Further south on a ridge stands the pale domed mausoleum of the Aga Khan, who died in 1957.
tour.story: The governors in those tombs ran the frontier more than four thousand years ago and led expeditions deep into Africa. The best story belongs to Harkhuf. On his fourth journey he sent word that he was bringing back a dancing pygmy from a faraway land. The king, Pepi the Second, was still a boy. He wrote back in excitement, and Harkhuf carved the royal letter on the front of his tomb: bring the dancer quickly, have men watch him on the boat so he does not fall in, and check on him ten times a night.
spot: The domed shrine on the hilltop
The Aga Khan's mausoleum to the south
tour.ask: Can we see Harkhuf's tomb door from the boat?

tour.title: The Nubian villages
tour.where: Ask whether the felucca lands. On Elephantine, the villages of Siou and Koti sit in the middle of the island. Gharb Soheil, the bigger visitor village, is on the west bank further south, usually by motorboat.
tour.look: Nubian houses are easy to recognise: thick walls, vaulted or domed roofs, and fronts painted white, blue, ochre or green, with patterns, palms or animals around the doors. On Elephantine the lanes are narrow and quiet; you walk between gardens and goats, and someone may offer you hibiscus tea.
tour.story: Whitewash keeps walls cooler, and the painted signs say who lives there and what they celebrate. When the lake rose, many families lost houses that had been theirs for generations. Nubian languages, Nobiin and Kenzi, are still spoken at home.
spot: Patterns made of plates or tiles
tour.photo: Photograph walls and doors freely; ask before photographing a person, and accept a no.
tour.ask: Is a village visit in our programme, or can we add one?

tour.title: Sunset on the water
tour.where: The last half hour of the ride, in the channel between Elephantine and the west bank, looking west to the dunes.
tour.look: The sun sets behind the west bank hills, a little south of due west at this time of year. First gold on the granite, then pink on the sand, then the sails become black triangles against the sky. Turn around: the low sun lights the east bank in orange. Fifteen minutes after sunset, look west again for the afterglow, often the best colour of all.
tour.story: For the Egyptians the west was the land of the dead, because the sun died there every evening. That is why the governors were buried on the west bank, on the hill in front of you, and why the royal tombs of Luxor are on the west bank too. You are watching it set from a boat on the Nile, which is exactly how an Egyptian pictured the end of the sun's day.
tour.photo: Tap the brightest part of the sky and slide the exposure down: black sails, red sky.

tour.title: Optional add-on: the Unfinished Obelisk
tour.where: Not in your programme. It lies in the old granite quarries in the southern part of town, a short drive from the river. Ask your guide whether it can fit.
tour.look: A giant obelisk lies on its back in the bedrock, still attached underneath. Look at the trenches around it: workers pounded them out with balls of a harder stone called dolerite. Then find the crack that crosses the shaft. That crack is why the obelisk stayed here.
tour.story: Finished, it would have been about forty-two metres long and weighed around eleven hundred tonnes, a third bigger than any obelisk Egypt raised. It is often linked to Hatshepsut, but nobody can prove who ordered it. When the granite cracked, the work stopped and stayed frozen in the rock: the step before every obelisk you saw at Karnak and Luxor.
spot: Ochre guide lines on the rock

alone.intro: On the dam the coach sets the time. The felucca is where you get time to yourselves. Once I have pointed out the landmarks, I will go quiet. A felucca ride is best when nobody talks: the sail creaks, the water slaps the hull, and the call to prayer drifts across from the town.

plans.d: Pick one side of the boat each. One watches Elephantine for the Nilometer stairs and the ruins, one watches the west bank for the tomb doorways and the hilltop dome, one counts birds. Swap after ten minutes. Then everyone takes one photograph only, the best they can, and you compare them at dinner.

Do the twenty-minute plan, then ask the captain whether one of the teenagers can hold the tiller or the rope for a few minutes under his eye. Learn the moment of a tack: the boat turns, the sail swings over, everyone ducks. Then sit at the front, look south to the boulders and imagine boats being hauled through the rapids.

plans.t: If you want one more thing
plans.d: Ask the captain to pass close under the west bank cliff to see the tomb doorways, or near Kitchener's Island for the birds. If the programme allows, ten minutes in a Nubian village lane on Elephantine is the best extra of the day.

alone.meet: On the felucca the boat is the meeting point. On the dam, repeat the coach departure time out loud as you get off and set a phone timer for five minutes before it.

details.d: On the High Dam, look at both sides within a minute. The lake stands far above the river below, and that drop drives the turbines.
As thanks for moving Kalabsha, Egypt gave West Germany a decorated gateway from the temple. It is now in Berlin.
Five concrete petals with a viewing platform at the top: a piece of Soviet design in the middle of Nubia.
Small boats around Aswan are painted with names and colours. Children sometimes paddle out and sing to visitors; a small coin is the usual thanks.
Many rocks around Elephantine and Sehel carry carved names and prayers left by officials. From the boat, look for squared panels on dark rock.
On the west bank cliff, the sloping lines below some tomb doors are ramps used to haul coffins up from the river.
The small dome on top of the west bank hill is a holy man's tomb and gives the hill its name, Qubbet el-Hawa.
Pied kingfishers, black and white, hover over the water and then dive. A slow felucca is the perfect seat.
The Nile here is blue-green because the silt stays in the lake. Before the dam, the flood ran brown and red.
Look at the sails around you. Many are patched like quilts, a record of years of work.

qa.q: Was the High Dam a good idea?
qa.a: Most Egyptians and historians would say necessary and costly. It protected Egypt from the 1980s drought, allowed year-round irrigation and doubled the country's electricity at the time. The costs are real: lost silt, coastal erosion, salty fields and the displacement of the Nubians. Engineers still debate how fast silt is filling the lake. A good dinner debate.

qa.q: Why is it called Lake Nasser?
qa.a: After Gamal Abdel Nasser, president of Egypt from 1956 until his death in 1970, who made the dam the symbol of his government. The Sudanese part is called Lake Nubia.

qa.q: Can the dam break?
qa.a: It is an embankment dam, a huge mass of rock and sand with a clay core, about 980 metres thick at its base. Dams like this are much less prone to sudden failure than thin concrete walls. Spillways can send surplus water into the desert to the west. It is guarded closely as a matter of national security.

qa.q: Are there crocodiles in the lake?
qa.a: Yes. Crocodiles vanished from the river below the dam long ago, but Lake Nasser has a large population because it is quiet and full of fish. You will not see them on the river at Aswan. Some homes in the visitor villages keep small crocodiles as a curiosity; whether that is a good idea is worth discussing.

qa.q: How does a felucca sail into the wind?
qa.a: It cannot sail straight into it. The captain points the boat at an angle to the wind, then turns and goes at the same angle on the other side. Each turn is a tack, and the boat moves upwind in a zigzag. Going north, the current helps, so a few tacks are usually enough.

qa.q: Who lived on Elephantine?
qa.a: Governors, priests, soldiers, traders and stone workers, over three thousand years. Old Kingdom governors led expeditions south. Under the Persian empire, around 500 to 400 BC, a garrison of Jewish soldiers lived here with their families and their own temple; their letters on papyrus are among the best records of daily life from that period.

qa.q: Why move the temples and not the people?
qa.a: Egypt did move the people, about fifty thousand Egyptian Nubians, to new villages near Kom Ombo, and Sudan moved its Nubians from around Wadi Halfa far to the east. Many say the new villages were built without listening to how they lived. The temples had international money and attention. Nubian views on this are strong and varied; ask your guide.

qa.q: What does Aswan mean?
qa.a: The name comes from the ancient Swenet, Syene in Greek, often explained as a word linked to trade, which suits a town living on goods passing between Egypt and Nubia. Scholars are not fully sure, so treat it as the best explanation available.

practical: The dam stop is about 45 minutes, with almost no shade. Hats on before you get off.
Photography on the dam is normally fine for visitors; drones are not. Ask your guide if unsure.
Take water onto the felucca, and use a toilet before boarding: there is none on board.
Sunscreen and hats: a felucca has little shade, and the water reflects the light.
Phones on a strap or in a zipped bag. A phone dropped here does not come back.
Sit where the captain asks and duck when he says the sail is swinging over.
Expect sellers at the quay. A smile and a clear 'la, shukran' (no, thank you) works.
The Unfinished Obelisk is not in your programme. Ask your guide early in the day if you want it.

kids.d: The dam is about 3,830 metres long. At 5 km per hour, how many minutes to walk across? It holds about 43 million cubic metres of fill: how many 10-cubic-metre truckloads is that?
Find a boulder in the river that looks like an elephant and photograph it. The family votes on the best one at dinner.
Spot an egret, a heron, a kingfisher, a pigeon and a crow. First to five wins. Bonus point for a hovering kingfisher.
Learn from the captain how a tack works, then explain it to your parents using your hand as the boat.
Draw one painted door with its colours and patterns, then design one for your own house in the same style.
