A wooden sailing boat with one triangular lateen sail.
The island opposite Aswan, the ancient town of Abu.
Ram-headed god of the cataract, who shaped people on a potter's wheel and released the flood.
Goddess of Elephantine and the flood, with a crown and antelope horns.
A stairway or well with marked levels, used to measure the river.
The Dome of the Wind, the west bank hill with the Tombs of the Nobles.

tonight: If one dam could save a country and drown a homeland, would you build it? What would you promise the people who lose their homes?
Harkhuf carved a letter from a child king on his tomb because he was proud of it. What would you carve on yours?
Which felucca photograph would you print and hang at home, and why?

sites.name: Philae, the temple that moved
sites.kicker: Day 7 morning · by motorboat to Agilkia Island
sites.hook: The sanctuary of Isis, dismantled block by block and rebuilt on higher ground in the 1970s.
facts: from about 380 BC to Roman times

story.title: The last hieroglyphs
story.text: Philae was the last of Egypt's temples to close. While Rome became Christian, pilgrims kept coming here to honour Isis, the mother goddess. The last dated hieroglyphic inscription we know of, from 24 August AD 394, is carved here. The temple was closed in the sixth century. Fifteen centuries later, the rising waters behind the dams threatened it again. Engineers built a wall around the island, pumped it dry, cut the temples into blocks, numbered them and rebuilt them on a neighbouring island that was shaped to look like the original.

steps: Motorboat ride from the landing to the island
The Kiosk of Nectanebo and the west colonnade
The First Pylon with the giant king figures
The court and the Birth House (Mammisi)
The Second Pylon and the hall
The inner sanctuary of Isis
The Gate of Hadrian and the Osiris rooms
Trajan's Kiosk by the water, the last view

dont_miss.d: The temple rises from the water. This is the view travellers painted in the nineteenth century.
Huge figures of a king smiting enemies in front of gods. The figures are scratched with early Christian crosses.
The last hieroglyphic inscription is nearby. Ask the guide where, and for the relief of the god of the Nile in his cave.
A Roman kiosk by the water, never finished. It is on every postcard.
Ask whether any building marks from the 1970s relocation are visible on the stones.

easy: Look closely at the reliefs on the pylons: some have Christian crosses carved on them.
The Birth House walls show Isis nursing the baby Horus.
Graffiti from 1799: French soldiers of Napoleon's expedition left an inscription at Philae. Ask the guide.
Look for the Nilometer at the foot of the island.
Agilkia Island was reshaped to resemble the original Philae. The old island is now under the lake.
ask: Who was Isis, and why did her worship spread to Rome?
Where is the old Philae island today?
How were the blocks numbered and moved?
What did the temple look like in colour?
Where is the French inscription from 1799?
quests: Look closer
Find a Christian cross carved on a temple wall. What does it tell you about how the temple was used after its gods left?
Estimate
Tens of thousands of blocks were moved. Say 40,000. If a crew moved 20 per day, how long would the job take? What would you want on your crew?
tips: Boats are small and the sun is bright. Hat, sunscreen, water.
The Sound and Light show at Philae is optional (65 EUR per person, in French, as listed in your programme).
Stone steps can be uneven. Watch your footing on the quay.

deep.guide_line: One island, one goddess, a thousand years of builders: I will walk you through it in the order the pilgrims did, then give you the island to yourselves.

briefing.intro: Philae is a sanctuary of Isis on a small island south of Aswan, between the old British dam and the High Dam. You reach it the way every pilgrim did, by boat. The island you land on is Agilkia: the temples were taken apart and rebuilt here between 1977 and 1980, because the original island was drowning. The story of the goddess and of the rescue is told in episode l05. This page is about the visit itself. We will land at the southern tip, walk north up a long court lined with columns, pass through two gateways into the temple of Isis and reach her dark sanctuary. Then we come out on the west side to a gate that faced the tomb of Osiris, and finish on the east shore at the most photographed kiosk in Egypt. Almost everything you see was built by Greek and Roman rulers dressed as pharaohs, from about 380 BC to the second century AD. It is compact, about an hour and a half with your guide, and it rewards slow looking.

know.d: The wife of Osiris and mother of Horus, the great magician and protector of children. Her name is written with a throne, and she often wears one on her head. Look for the little throne sign everywhere today. Episode l05 tells her story.

The oldest building here dates from Nectanebo the First, the last great native dynasty, around 380 to 362 BC. Most of the rest is Ptolemaic, built by the Greek kings descended from Alexander's general, and Roman. Some walls were left undecorated or half carved when work stopped.

Philae is a bent temple. The court, the first pylon, the second pylon and the sanctuary sit on slightly different angles, because builders followed the shape of the rock island over several centuries. Notice the turns as you walk.

know.t: Agilkia is a copy of a place
know.d: Engineers reshaped Agilkia, about 500 metres from the old island and higher, so its outline matched Philae's. The buildings face the same directions as before. The old island now lies under the water nearby.

After the temple closed in the sixth century, the hypostyle hall became a church. Crosses were carved into the old scenes and many faces of the gods were chipped away. That damage is part of the building's history.

Outside walls use sunk relief, carved into the surface, which casts strong shadows in sunlight. Inside walls use raised relief, where the background is cut away, which reads better in soft light. Run your eye along a wall and you can feel the difference.

The first pylon faces roughly south. In the morning the sun comes from the east and south-east, so the pylon and the court are lit from the side and the colonnades throw long stripes of shade. That is good for reliefs and for faces.

tour.title: The boat approach
tour.where: On the motorboat from the landing on the east bank. Sit on the side facing the island, and keep facing forward as you round the rocks.
tour.look: The island rises out of the water from the east. On the left you see a tall open pavilion of columns at the water's edge, Trajan's Kiosk. On the right, the twin towers of the temple of Isis. Between and around them, dark granite boulders of the cataract break the surface. Look past the island to the west for a bigger rocky island: Biga, where the Egyptians placed the tomb of Osiris.
tour.story: This is the view that made Philae famous. Nineteenth-century travellers called it the pearl of Egypt, and painters and photographers came for this angle. In 1968 the same view showed only the tops of the pylons above the water. The ride is short, so have your phone ready. The morning sun is behind you as you come in, which lights the temple fronts.
spot: The pylon towers on the right
tour.photo: Shoot from the boat as you round the rocks: kiosk left, pylons right, water in front.

tour.title: Landing and the Kiosk of Nectanebo
tour.where: Boats land near the southern tip. Walk up to the small roofless hall of columns at the tip of the island, facing north.
tour.look: This little hall is the oldest building on the island, a gateway pavilion of Nectanebo the First. It had fourteen columns; six stand. Look at the tops of the columns: some carry the face of Hathor with cow ears, on a shape like a sistrum, the rattle of the goddess. Look at the low screen walls between the columns: the king offering to the gods. From here the whole island stretches north in front of you.
tour.story: Pilgrims arriving by boat stepped up here and entered a sacred world. The pavilion was a vestibule to an older temple of Isis that the Ptolemies replaced. Nectanebo was one of the last Egyptian-born pharaohs before the Persians and then Alexander took over. Stand at the north end of the kiosk and look up the court: this is the walk the procession made.
tour.ask: Where exactly was the kiosk on the old island?

tour.title: The outer court and its two colonnades
tour.where: Walk north up the long open court. The long colonnade is on your left, the west; the shorter one on your right, the east.
tour.look: Count the columns on the west side: thirty-one remain of thirty-two, and every capital is different, palms, papyrus, lotus and mixed bouquets. Look on them for the Roman emperor Tiberius making offerings, and up for scraps of a ceiling of stars and vultures. The east colonnade was never finished: some capitals are only roughed out. Near its southern end stand small temples to Nubian gods, Arensnuphis and Mandulis. At its northern end is a small temple of Imhotep.
tour.story: Imhotep is the architect of the Step Pyramid you saw at Saqqara. Two thousand years after his death he was worshipped as a god of healing, and here he has his own temple. At the north end of the west colonnade, a Nilometer is cut into the bank. The temple measured the river that fed it.
spot: Unfinished capitals on the east side
tour.ask: Which capital is the oddest, and what plant is it?

tour.title: The First Pylon
tour.where: At the north end of the court, stand back near the two granite lions and face the great gateway, looking north.
tour.look: Two towers about eighteen metres high, with the gate between them. On each tower the king grips a bunch of enemies by the hair and raises his mace in front of the gods; it is Ptolemy the Twelfth. Higher up he offers to Isis and Horus. Look at the four tall grooves in the facade: flagpoles with banners stood in them. Find the small figures of Nile gods carrying offerings along the base. A smaller doorway in the eastern tower is older, from Nectanebo.
tour.story: The smiting scene is the oldest picture in Egyptian royal art, the king keeping chaos out of the temple. It did not need a real battle. The pink granite lions are later additions in a Roman style. Two granite obelisks once stood in front of this pylon. One was carried to England in the nineteenth century by the traveller William Bankes and still stands in a Dorset garden; episode l05 explains why it mattered for reading hieroglyphs.
spot: Chipped faces on the west tower
tour.photo: Family in front of the gate between the lions, photographer far enough back to fit the towers. See the photo list.

tour.title: The gate passage and the Birth House
tour.where: Walk through the central gateway. Inside the passage, look at the eastern wall, then step into the forecourt. The Birth House is on your left, the west.
tour.look: In the passage, find a neat block of French text carved in 1799 by Napoleon's soldiers, recording that General Desaix chased the Mamluks beyond the cataracts. Then the forecourt. On the west side stands the Birth House, the mammisi, surrounded by columns whose capitals carry the face of Hathor. On the east side, a colonnade fronts a row of rooms: storerooms, perhaps a library, and rooms for purification.
tour.story: A birth house celebrated the birth of the divine child, here Horus, son of Isis. Every year the priests replayed it, and with it the king's own right to rule. Inside, Horus is shown as a falcon in a papyrus thicket, hidden from Set, and Isis holds her newborn son.
spot: Hathor capitals on the Birth House
The rooms behind the east colonnade
tour.ask: Can you show us Isis nursing Horus in the Birth House?

tour.title: The Second Pylon and the granite stela
tour.where: Cross the forecourt to the second, smaller gateway. Look at the foot of its eastern tower, on your right as you face north.
tour.look: This pylon is smaller, about twelve metres high, and it is not parallel to the first one: you have just turned. At the base of the eastern tower, a lump of natural granite has been smoothed and carved. It is a piece of the original island's rock, worked into a stela by Ptolemy the Sixth, who stands with Queen Cleopatra the Second in front of Isis and Horus. Steps lead up into the gateway.
tour.story: The stela records a gift of land to Isis: the strip of the Nile valley south of here, called the Dodekaschoinos, the twelve-mile land, whose income went to the temple. When the temple moved, the engineers cut this piece of bedrock and moved it with the walls. Philae owned a slice of Nubia.
spot: The change of angle between pylons
tour.ask: How much land did Philae own, and who worked it?

tour.title: The hypostyle hall and the church
tour.where: Through the second pylon, into the covered hall of ten columns. Stand in the centre and look up, then at the walls.
tour.look: Here the colour survives: greens, blues and reds on the plant capitals, and on the ceiling the vultures of Upper and Lower Egypt with spread wings, and the boats of the sun. Now look lower at the walls and doorways: crosses carved into the old reliefs, and faces of gods cut away. Near a doorway, ask your guide to point out the Greek inscription of Bishop Theodore, who boasted of the good work of turning the temple into a church.
tour.story: Around the sixth century, this hall became a church dedicated to Saint Stephen. An altar stood here. The crosses claimed the building for a new faith, the way the old kings had claimed it with their names. Later inscriptions record visitors up to the nineteenth century, including a papal expedition in 1841.
tour.photo: Hold the phone flat against your chest, lens up, to photograph the ceiling without tilting.

tour.title: The sanctuary of Isis
tour.where: Walk straight on through the small rooms behind the hall to the last, narrow room at the back.
tour.look: The sanctuary is small and dim, with two little windows. In the middle stands a stone pedestal. It held the sacred boat carrying the statue of Isis and was given by Ptolemy the Third and his queen Berenice. On the walls, the king offers to Isis, who sometimes nurses Horus. Let your eyes adjust for a minute before you decide there is nothing to see.
tour.story: Only priests came in here. Every morning they opened the shrine, woke, washed, dressed and fed the goddess, then sealed it again. On feast days her statue left in its boat and crossed the water to Biga to visit Osiris. The real shrines that stood in this room are now in museums in Paris and Florence. Stairs near the second pylon lead to small chapels of Osiris on the roof, with scenes of his death and rebirth; they are often closed.
spot: Isis with the throne on her head
tour.ask: Are the Osiris chapels on the roof open today?

tour.title: The Gate of Hadrian
tour.where: Leave the temple by a side door on the west, or walk around the outside of the second pylon to the west side. The gate is a long passage on the western edge, facing Biga.
tour.look: In the passage, find the famous relief of the Nile's source: the river god Hapi crouches in a cave under a pile of rocks, wrapped by a snake, pouring water from two jars. On top of the rocks sits a falcon. Nearby, a scene shows a crocodile carrying the body of Osiris towards a rocky island. Above the door, the emperor Hadrian stands before the gods. Look out west across the water to Biga.
tour.story: This gate was the start of the procession to the tomb of Osiris on Biga, the Abaton, the place nobody could walk. The Egyptians imagined the flood rising from caverns at the cataract, under the very rocks you sailed through. Somewhere on this gate are the last hieroglyphs ever carved, from AD 394; episode l05 tells that story, so ask your guide to point to the small figure of Mandulis.
tour.ask: Where is the last hieroglyphic inscription, and can we see it?

tour.title: The temple of Hathor and Trajan's Kiosk
tour.where: Cross back to the east side of the island. A small temple of Hathor stands east of the temple of Isis; the kiosk is just south of it, on the edge of the water.
tour.look: In the little temple of Hathor, look for scenes of music and dance on the columns: musicians, and among them the dwarf god Bes. Then the kiosk: fourteen tall columns joined by low screen walls, each capital a different bundle of plants, and above them tall square blocks left blank. Only a couple of scenes were ever carved inside. The roof was timber and has gone, so the kiosk is open to the sky.
tour.story: The kiosk faced the river and was probably a grand landing hall, where the goddess's boat could rest on festival days. It carries the name of the emperor Trajan, around AD 100, but some of it may be older. The blank blocks above the capitals were meant to become faces of Bes and were never finished.
tour.photo: From the north-west corner of the kiosk, frame the columns with the water behind. Late morning, the sun is high enough not to blind you.

alone.intro: Here I leave you. The island is small: water on every side, the landing at the southern tip. Keep the time your guide gives you for the boat back. Below are four ways to use it.

plans.d: Go back into the hypostyle hall and look only up for two minutes, then at the crosses. Walk out to the Gate of Hadrian and find Hapi in his cave. End at the kiosk and sit on the low wall facing the water.

Start at the Birth House and find Horus in the papyrus. Walk the full west colonnade, counting capital shapes, and find the Nilometer at its north end. Then cross to the Hathor temple and look for Bes before ending at the kiosk.

plans.t: If you want one more thing
plans.d: Walk all the way around the outside of the temple of Isis. The outer walls carry huge scenes of Roman emperors as pharaohs, and the north end of the island is quieter, with views back to the pylons.

alone.meet: Meet at the kiosk ten minutes before the boat time, then walk together to the landing at the southern tip. The boats keep a schedule, so do not be the last family down.

details.d: Isis wears a small throne, the sign of her name. Count how many you see. On later scenes she often wears cow horns and a sun disc instead, borrowed from Hathor.
The cartouches of Augustus, Tiberius and other emperors are carved in hieroglyphs. Your guide can read 'Kaisaros', Caesar, in a cartouche.
On the east colonnade, some capitals are rough blocks. You can see the stages of carving from block to flower.
The architect of Saqqara has a temple here, built in the Ptolemaic period, two thousand years after his life.
Three Romans carved Latin graffiti on the first pylon in 116 BC, the oldest known Latin inscriptions in Egypt.
At the north end of the west colonnade, a stair cut into the bank measured the river. Even the goddess needed the flood report.
Look closely at walls for fine straight seams that cross the reliefs: some are the 1970s cuts, reassembled.
Names and dates of nineteenth-century visitors are carved in many places, some very neat. Find the oldest date you can.
On the outer face of the pylon the figures are sunk into the stone. Inside the hall they stand out from it. Feel the difference with your eyes.
The lower parts of some walls are paler or stained. Decades under the dam lake washed away the paint.

qa.q: Is this the real temple?
qa.a: Yes: the same stones, carvings and arrangement. Only the island is different. The engineers measured and numbered every block, cut the walls along lines chosen to avoid faces and texts where possible, and rebuilt them on Agilkia in the same orientation. What was lost is the ground itself and the original rock.

qa.q: Why are so many faces chipped?
qa.a: Mostly by Christians in late antiquity, who saw the gods as dangerous idols. Scholars note that the damage is often targeted, faces, hands, feet, as if to switch the images off. Some later damage came from visitors and from the years under water.

qa.q: Who built most of it?
qa.a: The Ptolemies, the Greek-speaking kings who ruled Egypt from Alexander's death to Cleopatra, then Roman emperors. Ptolemy II began the main temple, Ptolemy III completed much of it, and others added the birth house, the pylons and the decoration. Nectanebo I's kiosk is earlier, and Trajan's Kiosk later.

qa.q: Was the temple painted?
qa.a: Yes, all over. Reliefs were coloured in bright mineral paint. Nineteenth-century travellers still saw a lot of colour, especially in the hypostyle hall. Decades of flooding after 1902 washed much of it away. What survives on the capitals and ceiling hints at the rest.

qa.q: Why do Nubian gods appear here?
qa.a: Philae was on the border, and many of its worshippers came from Nubia, including the Blemmyes and Nobades who kept visiting even after Rome became Christian. Gods like Mandulis and Arensnuphis were honoured beside Isis, and Nubian kings of Meroe also sent gifts.

qa.q: How did they cut the blocks without breaking the carvings?
qa.a: With saws and careful planning. Each wall was photographed and drawn, cut lines chosen along joints or plain areas, and every block numbered. Blocks were lifted by crane, stored, and set back on Agilkia, with steel and mortar where needed. Ask your guide whether the cut lines are visible; on some walls they are.

qa.q: Did people live on the island?
qa.a: Priests, temple workers and later monks lived here, and the Christian period added churches and houses. The mud-brick houses and the small churches on the north side have mostly disappeared or were not rebuilt on Agilkia.

qa.q: Who was Bes?
qa.a: A dwarf god with a lion's mane and a protruding tongue, a protector of homes, mothers and babies, and a god of music and dance. He looks fierce to scare evil away. He is a favourite of children and appears often in birth houses.

At the Gate of Hadrian, find the god in his cave with the snake. How many jars is he pouring?
Sit in the shade of the Birth House and draw one Hathor capital: face, cow ears and the little house on top.
Was it right to carve crosses into the temple? Half the family argues for the monks, half for the old priests.

story.title: The sun that visits twice a year
story.text: Ramesses II had a temple cut into the cliff so that on two days in the year the rising sun reaches deep inside and lights the statues in the sanctuary. The dates are about 22 February and 22 October. After the temple was cut into blocks in the 1960s and moved to higher ground, the dates may have shifted by about a day. Your Day 8 is 28 October, so you will not see it. You will still see four seated colossi, each about 20 m high, and a smaller temple for his queen Nefertari.

deep.guide_line: If you make the early start, I will show you the biggest portrait of a king ever carved, the queen he set beside him, and the mountain built to hold them both.

briefing.intro: Abu Simbel is optional and it costs you a short night: the coach leaves Aswan in the small hours and drives about three hours south through empty desert, close to the Sudanese border. In return you get two temples cut into a sandstone cliff by Ramesses the Second around 1260 BC, on the edge of Lake Nasser. The Great Temple is his: four seated colossi of the king guard a doorway that runs about sixty metres into the rock. A hundred and fifty metres or so to the north, the Small Temple belongs to the goddess Hathor and to his queen Nefertari. Both temples were cut into blocks in the 1960s and rebuilt higher up, inside an artificial hill. The temples face east, so the morning light you arrive in is the light they were designed for. You will have about one and a half to two hours on site. Episode l03 tells the Battle of Kadesh; here we read it on the wall.

know.d: Abu Simbel stands in Nubia, the gold-rich land Egypt ruled south of Aswan. A colossal king carved into the cliff was a message to anyone sailing north on the river: this land belongs to Pharaoh. It was also a sacred place, and the cliff may have had older local cults.

He ruled about sixty-six years, around 1279 to 1213 BC, had over a hundred children and built more than any other pharaoh. At Abu Simbel he appears as a man, as a god, and even as a god worshipping himself. Episode l03 covers his reign and the Battle of Kadesh.

His first great royal wife, highly educated, shown with him on many monuments. She probably died around year twenty-five of his reign, close to when the temples were finished. Her beautiful tomb is in the Valley of the Queens, on your Day 10 page.

On about 22 February and 22 October, the rising sun shines down the axis of the Great Temple and lights three of the four statues in the sanctuary. Your visit on 28 October misses it by six days. The sun still lights the facade and the first hall in the morning.

From 1964 to 1968 an international team cut both temples into more than a thousand blocks, lifted them and rebuilt them 65 metres higher and about 200 metres back from the river, against two concrete domes covered by an artificial hill. Half the cost came from Egypt, half from dozens of other countries.

By 1800 sand covered most of the Great Temple. The Swiss traveller Burckhardt saw the top of the facade in 1813. The Italian strongman and explorer Belzoni dug down to the doorway and entered on 1 August 1817.

The road from Aswan runs about 280 km through desert, with a rest stop on the way. Coaches traditionally drive in a group with police escort. Sunrise on 28 October is around 6:55 am (Egypt is still on summer time until the night of 29 to 30 October).

tour.title: Around the hill to the lake
tour.where: From the visitor buildings, follow the path that curves around the hill. The lake opens up ahead and the temples appear on its shore, facing east.
tour.look: The hill beside you looks natural: rock, sand, a few boulders. It was built in the 1960s, a man-made mountain over two concrete domes, shaped to match the old cliff. Look at the lake: wide, blue and empty, with desert on the far shore. Then the temples come into view, the Great Temple to the south and the Small Temple to the north. Stop once before you get close. This is the only place you see both together with the water.
tour.story: The original cliff stood lower down, near the river, which is now under the lake in front of you. Travellers in the nineteenth century came by boat and saw the colossi from the water, half buried in a slope of sand that poured over the cliff. Belzoni needed weeks to dig down to the door.
spot: The lake where the old site lies
The shape of the artificial hill
tour.photo: Stop for one wide photo of both temples and the lake before you walk on.

tour.title: The Great Temple facade
tour.where: Stand on the open plaza about 40 metres in front of the Great Temple, facing west towards the doorway. South is on your left, north on your right.
tour.look: Four seated colossi of Ramesses, each about twenty metres, wearing the double crown. Above the doorway, in a niche, stands the falcon-headed sun god Ra-Horakhty, with a jackal-headed staff and a small goddess of truth at his sides. Read together they spell the king's throne name, User-maat-ra. At the very top, a row of seated baboons raises its arms to the rising sun. Count them: there were twenty-two.
tour.story: The facade was carved out of the living cliff; the joins you may see come from the 1960s move. Everything faces the sunrise. Baboons chatter at dawn, so the Egyptians saw them as greeting the sun. The king sits as an eternal guardian, while the god in the niche is both a statue of the sun and a giant signature of Ramesses.
spot: The falcon-headed god in the niche
The broken colossus south of the door
tour.ask: Which colossus is the best preserved, and why did the second one break?

tour.title: The colossi up close
tour.where: Walk to the feet of the colossi. Begin with the one immediately south of the door, on your left, whose head and body lie on the ground.
tour.look: Its upper half fell in an earthquake soon after the temple was finished; the pieces still lie where they landed. On its left leg, look for lines of small Greek letters: graffiti cut around 593 BC by Greek and Carian soldiers serving Psamtik the Second on a campaign into Nubia. Then look at the small standing figures between the legs: his queen Nefertari, his mother Tuya and some of his children. On the sides of the thrones, two Nile gods tie together the plants of Upper and Lower Egypt, and rows of bound prisoners line the bases.
tour.story: The Greek graffito reads like a soldiers' message: they came up the river as far as it allowed and carved their names. The family figures barely reach the king's knee. In Egyptian art, size means importance, and here even the queen mother is a small figure. Wait until you reach the Small Temple to see that change.
spot: Greek letters on the left leg
The fallen head on the ground
Nefertari and Tuya by the legs
tour.photo: Put one family member next to the fallen head for scale. Photographer back at 10 metres.
tour.ask: Which children are named between the legs?

tour.title: The great hall of Osiris pillars
tour.where: Go through the doorway. Stop just inside and let your eyes adjust; you are facing west, deep into the cliff.
tour.look: Eight pillars, in two rows of four, each with a standing statue of Ramesses as Osiris, arms crossed, about ten metres tall. Those on the south side, your left, wear the white crown of Upper Egypt; those on the north side, your right, the double crown. Look up: vultures with spread wings fly down the central aisle of the ceiling. The walls are covered with battle scenes, with colour still on some of them.
tour.story: Osiris was the king of the dead and of rebirth. By showing himself as Osiris, Ramesses told visitors that he would live for ever. The hall is cut from solid rock: nothing here was built, everything was carved out, which means the sculptors removed the space as much as they made the statues.
tour.ask: Are the pillar statues all identical, or can you spot differences?

tour.title: The Kadesh wall and the side rooms
tour.where: Turn to the north wall, on your right as you face into the temple. Then glance at the south wall opposite and at the doorways to the side rooms.
tour.look: The whole north wall is the Battle of Kadesh, about 1274 BC. Read it like a comic strip. At the bottom, the Egyptian army marches. In the middle, the camp, drawn as a rectangle of shields, with soldiers resting, horses and chariots. Two enemy scouts are beaten until they confess. On the right, the king charges alone in his chariot, bigger than everyone, and Hittite chariots crash around a river. The south wall shows other wars: the king storming a fortress and trampling a Libyan.
tour.story: Episode l03 tells how Kadesh was a near disaster and a draw, presented as a glorious victory. Here you can test that against the picture. The side rooms off the hall were storerooms for temple equipment and offerings; their walls are plainer and some were left rougher. Peek in if they are open.
spot: The king alone in his chariot
The fortress on the south wall
tour.ask: Where on this wall is the city of Kadesh itself?

tour.title: The sanctuary
tour.where: Walk straight on through the second, smaller hall with four pillars and the narrow vestibule, to the small room at the back.
tour.look: Four seated statues sit against the back wall, cut from the rock: Ptah, Amun-Ra, the deified Ramesses and Ra-Horakhty. In the second hall on the way, look for Ramesses and Nefertari before the sacred boat. In the sanctuary, find the stone base where the god's boat rested. Ptah, at the end of the row, is the god of craftsmen and of Memphis, linked with the underworld.
tour.story: On the alignment mornings in February and October, the first rays travel about sixty metres down the axis and light three of the four statues. Ptah, linked with darkness, stays in shadow. Whether the dates once marked the king's jubilee or his birthday is a popular idea that scholars do not confirm. The alignment survived the move to within about a day, which is remarkable after cutting and rebuilding the whole temple.
tour.ask: Which statue is Ptah, and which ones does the sun reach?

tour.title: The Small Temple facade
tour.where: Walk north along the plaza to the second temple. Stand about 30 metres back, facing west.
tour.look: Six standing statues about ten metres tall, set between buttresses: four of Ramesses, two of Nefertari. She wears the crown of Hathor, cow horns around a sun disc with two tall plumes. Each statue has small children at its sides, princes by the king, princesses by the queen. On the buttresses, inscriptions name the builder and the queen.
tour.story: This is one of very few temple facades where a queen stands at the same size as the king. A line on the facade is often translated as saying that Ramesses made this temple for his great royal wife Nefertari, for whose sake the sun rises. Hathor was the goddess of love, music and motherhood. By joining Nefertari to her, the temple made the queen almost divine during her lifetime.
spot: Nefertari at the same size as the king
tour.photo: Line the family up with the statues: four of you match the kings, two the queens.

tour.title: Inside Nefertari's temple
tour.where: Enter the hall of six square pillars, facing west. Then walk on to the small sanctuary at the back.
tour.look: The pillars carry the face of Hathor at the top, with cow ears, and below it the goddess and the queen with her rattle, the sistrum. The walls are lighter and gentler than the Great Temple: the queen offers flowers, plays music, and in a well-known scene two goddesses, Hathor and Isis, place a crown on her head. In the sanctuary niche, Hathor as a cow seems to step out of the rock, protecting the king.
tour.story: The same king who smites enemies on every wall nearby is shown here, with Nefertari behind him, but the mood is different. This temple is about the goddess and the queen. Nefertari's slim figure, fine dress and calm face are among the most elegant carvings of the reign.
spot: The cow emerging from the rock
tour.ask: Is the crowning scene of Nefertari here, and who is crowning her?

tour.title: The seams of the move
tour.where: Back outside, stand to one side of the Great Temple facade and look at the colossi's faces and chests from an angle.
tour.look: Look for fine straight lines crossing the faces, the crowns and the chests. These are the cuts made in 1965 and 1966, when the facade was sawn into blocks, and later filled with mortar. Once you see one, you see them everywhere.
tour.story: Facade cuts were made by hand saw, to keep them as thin as possible, and placed where the damage would be least visible. The heads were lifted out whole. A famous photograph from 1967 shows a colossus's face hanging from a crane, being set back in place. Behind the facade, a concrete dome about 55 metres across carries the weight of the hill, so the temple rooms are no longer holding up the mountain.
spot: The edge of the artificial hill
tour.ask: Is there any way to see inside the dome?

alone.intro: Here I leave you for the rest of your time on site. Both temples are a short walk apart on the same plaza, and the visitor buildings are behind the hill. Keep an eye on the coach time: the convoy waits for no one.

plans.d: Go back into the Great Temple alone, walk slowly to the sanctuary without stopping, then turn around and look back at the bright doorway from the darkness. That view, the light coming down the axis, is the whole idea of the temple. Then sit on the plaza facing the facade for five quiet minutes.

Do the twenty-minute plan, then go into Nefertari's temple a second time and find the crowning scene and the cow of Hathor. Walk to the lakeside edge of the plaza, look back at both facades and find the saw cuts on the colossi's faces.

plans.t: If you want one more thing
plans.d: Ask whether the small exhibition about the rescue in the visitor area is open: models and photographs show how the temples were cut and lifted. It makes the walk back around the hill much more interesting.

details.d: The frieze at the top of the Great Temple facade shows baboons greeting the sunrise. Count them from the plaza.
The god in the niche holds symbols that spell User-maat-ra, the king's throne name. The whole niche is a signature.
Near the facade, a stela records Ramesses' marriage to a Hittite princess after the peace treaty, about 1245 BC.
On the bases of the colossi, bound prisoners are carved: Nubians and Asiatics, the enemies of the south and the north.
Besides the Greek text, there are Carian and Phoenician graffiti, and nineteenth-century travellers' names carved high up, from when sand reached their level.
In the second hall and the sanctuary, look for the king offering to a god who is himself, with his own face.
Traces of red, yellow and blue survive on the walls and pillars of the Great Temple. Look along the edges of the figures.
In the Small Temple, the queen shakes a sistrum, a rattle with metal discs, to please Hathor. It is drawn like the Hathor pillars themselves.
North of the Great Temple facade, a small open-air chapel of the sun with baboon statues was cleared in 1909 to 1910. Ask if you can see it.
A door in the side of the hill leads to the space between the dome and the temple. It is normally closed to visitors.

qa.q: Why did Ramesses build so far south?
qa.a: To mark the land. Nubia supplied gold, stone, cattle and soldiers, and Egypt had ruled it for centuries. A temple with four colossi of the king, facing the river, was a permanent statement of power. The site may also have been sacred before him. Scholars also point out that he built several temples in Nubia, so Abu Simbel was the grandest of a series.

qa.q: How long did it take to carve?
qa.a: About twenty years is the usual estimate, from early in the reign to around year twenty-four or later. It was rock-cutting: workers removed the cliff from the outside in, leaving the statues and walls standing. Decoration went on afterwards, and the earthquake damage came soon after completion.

qa.q: Why does the sun only reach the sanctuary on two days?
qa.a: Because the sun rises at a slightly different point on the horizon each day. The temple axis points at the place where it rises around 22 February and 22 October. In between, the light falls short or to the side. Popular explanations link the days to the king's birthday and coronation, but there is no ancient text that says so.

qa.q: Did the move shift the alignment?
qa.a: Only slightly. The engineers kept the orientation, but the new site is higher and the horizon is different, so the date and the exact angle of the beam changed a little. Sources say the dates moved by about a day; others say the original dates are uncertain anyway. It still works, which is the remarkable part.

qa.q: Why not leave the temples where they were and build a dam around them?
qa.a: That was one of the proposals, along with lifting the whole temple on hydraulic jacks and leaving it under water to be seen from viewing chambers. The jacking plan was considered very expensive and risky, a wall around it would have needed pumping for ever, and underwater viewing would have left the temple in the dark. Cutting and moving was judged the safest and cheapest.

qa.q: Was Nefertari really equal to the king?
qa.a: Not politically. Ramesses held the power. But giving a queen statues of the same size on a temple facade was very rare and marks her special status. She appears with him at many temples and wrote to the Hittite queen in her own name. The Small Temple is the strongest sign of how much she mattered.

qa.q: Are those really Greek graffiti from 2,600 years ago?
qa.a: Yes. Around 593 BC, the pharaoh Psamtik the Second sent an army into Nubia that included Greek and Carian mercenaries. Some of them carved their names and a short account on the leg of the fallen colossus. The text is one of the earliest securely dated Greek inscriptions anywhere.

qa.q: What happens if Lake Nasser rises again?
qa.a: The temples now stand about 65 metres above their original level, above the highest planned water of the lake. The domes and the hill are monitored for cracks and movement. Damp and salt in the rock remain the long-term risks, more than the water itself.

practical: Decide the evening before. The coach leaves Aswan in the very early hours, often around 4 am; ask your representative for the exact time.
Programme prices: about 130 EUR per person by coach, 415 by plane. Children's prices are not listed; ask the representative.
Bring a fleece for the cold desert dawn and a hat for later. It warms up fast after 9 am.
The drive is about three hours each way. Sleep on the coach; downloaded episodes w09 and w10 are made for the last half hour.
Toilets are at the visitor area, not by the temples. Use them before you walk around the hill.
Time on site is short, about 1.5 to 2 hours. Do the Great Temple first, then the Small Temple.
Photography rules inside the temples have changed over the years. Check on the day; never use flash.
The long sail back from Aswan starts after you return, so expect a tired afternoon. Plan a nap.

kids.d: Count the baboons on top of the Great Temple facade. Do you get twenty-two? How many are damaged?
Find Nefertari and the king's mother between the legs of the colossi. How high do they reach on the king's leg?
On the leg of the broken colossus, find the Greek letters. Teenagers: can you spot any letter you know, like an alpha or a sigma?
Photograph the Small Temple facade and mark the queen and the king. Then find another temple from the trip where the queen is the same size. Can you?
Explain to your parents how the temple was moved: blocks, numbers, crane, dome. Use sugar cubes at breakfast to show it.

glossary.d: The site's modern name; the ancient temple was called the Temple of Ramesses, beloved of Amun.
Ramesses the Second, the builder, who ruled for about sixty-six years.
His first great royal wife. The name means beautiful companion.
Goddess of love, music and motherhood, shown as a cow or a woman with cow horns.
The rising sun, a falcon-headed god, Horus of the horizon.
A pillar with a statue of the king as Osiris in front of it.
A city in Syria where Ramesses fought the Hittites around 1274 BC.
A sacred rattle shaken for Hathor.

tonight: Is a temple still the same temple after being sawn into a thousand pieces and rebuilt 65 metres higher?
Ramesses put his queen at his own size on her temple. What does that tell you about him, or about her?
If you had to choose between saving Abu Simbel and saving a Nubian village, which would you choose, and why?

sites.name: Valley of the Queens and the Colossi of Memnon
sites.hook: Painted tombs for queens and princes, and two giant statues that once made a sound at dawn.
facts: Tombs about 1250-1150 BC, statues about 1350 BC
Princes with a side-lock of youth

story.title: The statue that sang
story.text: In 27 BC an earthquake cracked one of the two statues of Amenhotep III. At dawn it began to give out a low sound, a kind of whistle or hum, probably as the cooled stone warmed in the morning sun. The Greeks said it was Memnon, son of the Dawn goddess, greeting his mother. Roman tourists came for centuries to hear it and scratched their names into the legs, including the emperor Hadrian in AD 130. Around AD 200 another emperor repaired the crack and the voice was lost.

steps: Colossi of Memnon: a short photo stop on the way
Valley of the Queens: the visitor area
Tombs that are open that day (ask which)
Look for painted ceilings and the sides of doorways

dont_miss.d: About 18 m tall, each cut from a single block. They guarded the entrance of a vast temple that is now fields.
Zoom in on the stone: Roman visitors carved their names almost two thousand years ago.
Colour survives in tombs better than in temples, because the light never got in. Ask which are open.
Children are shown with one braid at the side of the head, called the side-lock of youth.

easy: Tombs of royal children are among the sweetest. Some princes died young and their father is shown leading them to the gods.
The quartzite for the Colossi came from near modern Cairo, nearly 700 km away.
The 'temple' behind the Colossi has almost completely vanished. The Memphis lesson again.
Look at the ceilings: many are painted deep blue with yellow stars, to turn the tomb into a night sky.
ask: Which tombs are open today, and are they included in our ticket?
Who was buried here, and what do their names mean?
Where is Nefertari's tomb, and can we see it?
How did the statue make a sound, and what do scientists say?
Where did the stone for the Colossi come from, and how did it travel?
quests: Look closer
Find a prince with the side-lock of youth. What is he doing with his hands?
Debate
A statue whistled at dawn and tourists came for 200 years. Then someone repaired it and the tourists left. Was the repair a mistake?
tips: Open tombs change daily and extra tickets may apply. Ask the guide, and do not expect a promise.
The Valley of the Kings is not on your printed programme. Ask if it is possible to add it. It sits beyond the same hills as Hatshepsut.
Heat is strong from mid-morning. Do the tombs first, shade second.

deep.guide_line: Two stone giants by the road, then the painted tombs of princes and queens, and by the end you will read a tomb wall on your own.

briefing.intro: Day 10 starts on the road. The coach crosses the green fields of the west bank and stops beside two seated giants, the Colossi of Memnon. Twenty minutes is enough if you know where to look. Then we drive on towards the cliffs, into a dry valley the Egyptians called Ta-Set-Neferu. Between about 1550 and 1130 BC they cut tombs here for royal wives and for the king's children; the kings lay in a bigger valley over the hill. These tombs are small, but several are among the best painted in Egypt, because daylight never reached them. A tomb was a machine for eternal life: its walls show the dead person introduced to the gods, passing guarded gates and arriving safely. Once you know the code, each wall reads like a page. The plan: the Colossi, the valley, then the tombs open that day, usually three on the standard ticket, plus Nefertari if you buy the separate ticket. About ten minutes inside each. Go early, drink often.

know.t: A valley of children as much as queens
know.d: Ta-Set-Neferu can be read as 'the place of beauty' or 'the place of the royal children'. About 110 tombs are known. The famous painted ones date from Ramesses I to Ramesses III, for queens and for princes who died before their father.

Each tomb has a QV number, for Queens' Valley, given in order of recording. QV66 is Nefertari, QV55 Prince Amunherkhepeshef, QV44 Prince Khaemwaset, QV52 Queen Tyti. The sign at each door gives the number, the owner and a plan.

Usually three or four tombs are open on the general ticket, rotated to let them rest. QV44, QV52 and QV55 have often been among them. Nefertari needs a separate, much more expensive ticket, with limited time inside. Ask your guide what is open today and check prices on the day.

The valley is cut into limestone, marl and shale that crumble and swell when wet. So walls were coated with plaster, carved in low relief in the plaster, then painted. Bare patches are where plaster fell. Salt and humidity are the enemies, and your breath is humidity.

In the princes' tombs the main figure is often their father, Ramesses III. He walks in front, introducing his son to each god. The prince follows, small, with the side-lock of youth. Nobody knows how old the princes were when they died, or why.

A handful of pigments did almost everything: red and yellow ochre from desert earth, white from gypsum, black from soot, and blue and green from Egyptian blue, a man-made pigment of copper, sand and lime fired in a kiln. It is often called the oldest synthetic pigment in the world.

Flash is banned in tombs: bursts of light fade pigment. Rules on phone photos inside have changed several times in recent years, and Nefertari has had its own rule. Ask at the ticket office or ask your guide before lifting a phone. Outside, photograph freely.

know.t: The Colossi guarded a vanished temple
know.d: The two statues stood at the gate of the memorial temple of Amenhotep III, built about 1350 BC, perhaps the largest ever built on the west bank. Floods, an earthquake and later builders took it apart. The story of the singing statue is in episode s11; here we look at the stone.

tour.title: The Colossi from the road
tour.where: Walk to the fenced area in front of the statues. They face east, towards the river, so you meet them face to face.
tour.look: Two seated kings, both Amenhotep III, hands flat on their knees, staring over your head at the sunrise. The faces are almost gone, worn by wind, sand and centuries of flood water. Compare them. The southern statue, on your left, is one block from head to throne. The northern one, on your right, has a body of stacked courses of stone, like a wall: the Roman repair. Now look through the fence behind them: low mounds, fallen statues on their backs, work tents. That field is the temple.
tour.story: These two never stood alone. They flanked the first gateway of a temple whose courts ran back towards the hills for hundreds of metres, full of statues. It was built on low ground near the river, perhaps on purpose, so the yearly flood would enter the courts like the waters of creation. That may have doomed it. Floods softened the foundations, an earthquake brought walls down, and later kings took the blocks. Since the late 1990s a mission has been digging and standing broken statues back up.
spot: The stacked repair blocks on the northern statue
Fallen statues in the field behind
The width of a throne compared with a person

tour.title: Thrones and visitors' names
tour.where: Walk along the fence to the side of a throne, then to the front of the northern statue.
tour.look: By the king's legs stand much smaller women: on the southern statue, his wife Tiye and his mother Mutemwia. They reach his knee. Size here means rank. On the sides of the thrones, two plump figures tie papyrus and lotus stems around a tall sign. They are Hapy, the flood god, binding the plants of north and south around the hieroglyph for 'unite': the king holds the Two Lands together. Then the legs of the northern statue: scratched Greek and Latin letters, left by Roman tourists.
tour.story: Quartzite was the hardest, most prized building stone the Egyptians used, and its red-gold colour was linked to the sun. It came from near modern Cairo, nearly seven hundred kilometres north. How blocks this size travelled is still debated: barges on the flood, sledges on wetted tracks, or both. The names on the legs date from Roman times, when the statue was famous for a sound at dawn. More than a hundred inscriptions survive, some just a name and 'I heard Memnon', some full poems.
spot: Tiye's small figure by the king's leg
Hapy tying the plants on a throne side
Greek letters on the northern legs
tour.photo: Zoom 2x or 3x on the legs in side light: the letters only show when light skims across them.
tour.ask: Can you show us one Greek inscription and read the name?

tour.title: Arriving in the valley
tour.where: From the coach park, walk up past the ticket check and the visitor building. The path climbs gently between low cliffs of pale stone.
tour.look: Stop before the first tomb and look around. This is a dry wadi, cut by rare, violent flash floods. The cliffs are layered like a cake, pale limestone over greyer, crumbly beds. Notice how small everything is compared with the temples. No pylon, no obelisk. Everything that mattered was underground and painted.
tour.story: From 1903 an Italian team under Ernesto Schiaparelli, director of the Egyptian Museum in Turin, worked through this valley tomb by tomb. Almost everything had been robbed in antiquity, and many tombs were packed with later burials. But the walls survived, and in 1904 they opened Nefertari's tomb. Romans later buried their dead here, and Coptic Christians lived in some tombs and painted crosses on the plaster.
spot: The layered colours of the cliff
The QV number plates at each door
Low walls that steer flood water away from doors
tour.ask: Which tombs are open today, and why are the others closed?

tour.title: How to read a tomb
tour.where: Stand in the shade by the first open tomb while your guide shows the tickets. One minute here pays for the whole morning.
tour.look: Four rules. One: the dead person walks in, from daylight to the burial chamber, so their figure usually faces inwards, and the gods usually face out to receive them. Two: hieroglyphs face the same way as the figure they belong to; start reading from the side the faces look towards. Three: oval rings, cartouches, hold royal names. Four: look up. The ceiling is the sky, deep blue with stars. Doorways matter most, with winged goddesses over them.
tour.story: A tomb is a text you walk through. In the corridors the dead person is presented to the great gods, as at a royal court. Deeper in, the route reaches the gates of the realm of Osiris. Each gate has a guardian, often animal-headed and holding a knife, and the dead must know its name to pass. The spells come from the Book of the Dead and similar guidebooks. In the burial chamber, Isis and Nephthys protect the dead, who becomes one with Osiris. You make the same trip, in the same direction.

tour.title: QV44, Prince Khaemwaset
tour.where: If it is open: a ramp down to a corridor with two side rooms, a second corridor, then the burial chamber.
tour.look: The first figure you meet is Ramesses III; his son comes behind. The king offers to Ptah, Thoth, Anubis and other gods, with the prince small behind him. Find the boy's side-lock, a thick braid over the ear. In the second corridor the prince appears dressed as a priest, among the guardians of the underworld. In the side rooms look for the four sons of Horus, with human, baboon, jackal and falcon heads, who guarded the dead person's organs.
tour.story: This Khaemwaset is a son of Ramesses III, a century younger than the famous Khaemwaset son of Ramesses II, the prince sometimes called the first Egyptologist. The tomb was found in February 1903, open and wrecked, and holding more than forty wooden coffins of later people placed here centuries after the prince. A damaged granite sarcophagus survives. We do not know how old he was when he died.
spot: The prince dressed as a priest
tour.ask: Why does the king take more space than his son in the son's own tomb?

tour.title: QV55, Prince Amunherkhepeshef
tour.where: A long entrance ramp leads to a first chamber with a side room, then a corridor and the burial chamber.
tour.look: His name means 'Amun is with his strong arm'. Another son of Ramesses III, and often the brightest painting of the day. Find the scene where Hathor leads the king by the hand, the prince behind with his side-lock and a tall fan. At the inner doorway Isis and Nephthys kneel to welcome the dead. In the corridor count the gate guardians: four, with knives, from chapter 145 of the Book of the Dead. A granite sarcophagus stands in the burial chamber.
tour.story: The Italian mission found the tomb in 1904, robbed long before. One thing surprises visitors: in a side room, a small glass case has held the mummified body of a foetus. It is not part of the prince's burial. It was found in another tomb nearby and placed here around 1974, then moved within the tomb in 2010. Guides sometimes tell a romantic story about it; nobody knows whose child it was. Warn the younger ones before going in. Some will want to look, some will not.
tour.ask: Is the foetus still shown, and what do we really know about it?

tour.title: QV52, Queen Tyti
tour.where: If it is open: a corridor to a central chamber with a small room off each side and one at the back, a cross-shaped plan.
tour.look: Here the owner is the star. Tyti shakes a sistrum, a rattle used in the worship of Hathor. The ceiling has white stars on a gridded ground. On the doorways, look for odd guardians, including a group of monkeys. The image to find is in a side room: Hathor twice, once as a goddess in a tree pouring water for the queen, once as a cow stepping out of the western mountain. That mountain is the hill above you.
tour.story: Tyti carries four titles: king's daughter, king's sister, king's wife and king's mother. Born to a king, married to a king, mother of a king. Which kings? The most accepted answer, from a papyrus list, makes her a wife of Ramesses III and mother of Ramesses IV, but a missing cartouche in the tomb prevents certainty.
spot: The cow coming out of the mountain
The sistrum in the queen's hand
tour.ask: Why would a queen want to be shown with Hathor as a cow?

tour.title: QV66, Nefertari (separate ticket)
tour.where: Up a short side path, under a shelter, where a guard controls entry and time. Stairs lead down to a suite of rooms, then a second stair to the four-pillared burial chamber.
tour.look: People who have seen every tomb in Egypt stop talking here. White plaster carved in low relief, painted with very fine detail. Nefertari wears a transparent white dress and a vulture headdress. Look for her playing senet alone: a board game against fate, for her life. Find the scarab god Khepri, the sun at dawn. Overhead, a deep blue ceiling with yellow stars. In the burial chamber, the pillars carry Osiris and priests.
tour.story: Nefertari was the Great Royal Wife of Ramesses II, whose small temple you may see at Abu Simbel. Schiaparelli found the tomb in 1904, robbed, with pieces of a sarcophagus lid, sandals and a pair of mummified knees; a 2016 study concluded the knees are probably hers. By the 1980s salt crystals were pushing the paint off. From 1986 to 1992 the Getty Conservation Institute and the Egyptian antiquities service secured and cleaned it, without repainting.
tour.ask: How long can we stay, and are phone photos allowed with this ticket?

alone.intro: The valley is small and the paths are walled, so nobody gets lost. I will wait near the visitor building while you visit the remaining open tombs at your own pace. Inside, keep voices low and let other groups pass in the narrow corridors.

plans.d: Pick one open tomb you have not seen and go in as a family, with nobody talking you through it. Use the four reading rules: who walks in, who faces out, where the gates are, what is on the ceiling. Come out, sit in the shade, and have each person name the one figure they would keep if every other wall vanished.

Go back into your favourite tomb and spend the whole visit on one wall: count the figures, find one cartouche, find a guardian's knife. Then walk slowly up the main path as far as it is open, past the numbered doors and the layered cliff, and turn round for the view down the valley to the fields.

Stop. Sit in the shade of the visitor building, drink a full bottle each, eat something salty. Tombs are warm and airless, so do not chain three in a row: one tomb, then ten minutes of shade, then the next.

alone.meet: Meet at the visitor building, in the shade, at the time your guide gives. Set a phone alarm five minutes before: inside a tomb you lose all sense of time.

photos.where: South-east corner of the viewing area, so the southern statue is near and the northern one steps back.
photos.when: Early morning, when the sun from the east-south-east lights their fronts.
photos.how: Phone at hip height, tilted up a little so they tower. Stay at 1x so they stay straight.
photos.avoid: Coaches and stalls on the road edge; turn until they leave the frame.

photos.t: The family at the feet of a giant
photos.where: In front of the fence, beside the southern statue, family turned at an angle to it.
photos.when: Morning. Facing east they would squint, so turn them until the sun comes from one side.
photos.how: Photographer 15 to 20 metres back so the whole statue fits above the family. One line, tallest at the edge. Tap a face to set exposure.
photos.avoid: The sun right behind the family; fence posts cutting through heads.

photos.where: Beside the northern statue's base, as close as the fence allows.
photos.when: Any time.
photos.how: One person reaches up as if to touch the knee; the photographer crouches low.
photos.avoid: Climbing on the fence or base. It is forbidden.

photos.where: Lower legs of the northern statue.
photos.when: Morning, with the sun skimming the stone from the side.
photos.how: Zoom 2x to 3x on one block of letters; slightly under-expose so the letters cast shadows.
photos.avoid: Flat midday light, when the letters disappear.

photos.where: On the main path just above the visitor building, looking up the valley.
photos.when: Mid-morning, before the light turns white.
photos.how: Horizontal, cliffs in the top third. Wait for a gap between groups.
photos.avoid: The sun straight ahead; move until it is to one side.

photos.where: Beside a stone door frame after your group comes out, against plain rock.
photos.when: When the doorway is in shade.
photos.how: Portrait mode, subject a step away from the rock; tap to expose for the face.
photos.avoid: Blocking the entrance. Ten seconds and move.

photos.where: Inside, under a blue ceiling with stars, standing on the wooden floor.
photos.when: Whenever you are inside; the lighting is fixed.
photos.how: No flash. Elbows tucked in, breath held, two or three frames.
photos.avoid: Leaning on a wall to steady yourself.

details.d: The Colossi's platforms sit below today's ground. Three thousand years of Nile silt raised the fields. The flood reached their feet until the Aswan dams stopped it.
The flood god has a belly and breasts: signs of plenty, the fat of a good harvest. He is male. Children always ask.
A tall fan on a pole marks a high court post. 'Fan-bearer on the right of the king' was a real title, so even a royal child carries one.
Men are painted reddish brown, women paler yellow. It is an artistic convention.
Where plaster has fallen, look at its edge. It can be a few millimetres thick. Everything you admire sits on that skin.
The glass panels on lower walls and the raised wooden floors exist because bags and hands rubbed paint away.
Look for red outline drawings never painted, or carving that stops. Work ended on the day of the funeral.
Christians later lived in some tombs. Ask if any open tomb today shows a cross or Christian graffiti.
In the princes' tombs, find the cartouche of Ramesses III with the small seated goddess Maat inside: Usermaatre.
Isis and Nephthys kneel on or hold signs for water or gold, offering what the dead need for the journey.

qa.q: Why are tomb paintings so bright when temples lost their colour?
qa.a: No sunlight: ultraviolet breaks pigments down, and these walls lived in the dark. No rain, and for long stretches no visitors. The pigments are minerals, stable for millennia if left alone. The threats came later: salt in the rock, flash floods, the humidity of crowds, hands and bags.

qa.q: Why are princes buried here and not with their father?
qa.a: The Valley of the Kings was, with few exceptions, for kings. Under the Ramesside kings this valley took royal wives and several of the king's children. Ramesses III built a group of tombs here for his sons. In them, the king presents each son to the gods, as if a father had to take his child by the hand into the afterlife.

qa.q: Did the princes die as children?
qa.a: We do not know. The side-lock of youth points to children, but adult priests in some roles wear it too, and some princes hold court titles. Some may have died young, some as young men; the paintings show an ideal youth either way.

qa.q: Who was Nefertari?
qa.a: The first Great Royal Wife of Ramesses II, married before he became king and mother of several of his children. She appears beside him on many monuments, and the small temple at Abu Simbel is dedicated to her and Hathor. A letter from her to the Hittite queen survives, from the diplomacy after the Battle of Kadesh.

qa.q: Is Nefertari's tomb worth the extra ticket?
qa.a: Your call. It is the best-preserved painted tomb most visitors can enter, finer than the other open tombs. Against it: a high price, limited time inside, possible queues. Check price and rules on the day.

qa.q: How did the painters see in the dark?
qa.a: With oil lamps, wicks floating in bowls of oil, possibly with salt added to cut smoke. Ceilings show surprisingly little soot. People often say mirrors reflected sunlight inside, but there is no direct evidence of that in tombs. Lamps are certain; mirrors remain an idea.

qa.q: How did the Colossus make a sound?
qa.a: The usual theory: after the earthquake of 27 BC cracked the northern statue, the morning sun warmed the stone and dried moisture in the cracks, producing a short note. Nobody measured it, so it stays a theory. After the Roman repair, around AD 200, the sound stopped.

qa.q: Why do guards offer to show things for a tip?
qa.a: Wages are low and tips are part of life at every site. A guard may offer to light a corner, open a closed room or allow a forbidden photo. A polite 'la, shukran', no thank you, is enough. Forbidden photos can bring a fine and harm the paint. A small tip for a real kindness is normal.

practical: Order: Colossi early, then the valley before the mid-morning heat. Your guide sets the actual order.
About 20 minutes at the Colossi, 1 to 1.5 hours in the valley.
Little shade outside apart from the visitor building: hats, sunscreen, sunglasses.
Tombs are warm and humid inside. Light, breathable clothes.
Water for everyone; drink before each tomb.
Closed shoes with grip: ramps are steep, with wooden floors and steps.
Toilets are usually at the visitor building. Use them before the first tomb.
Bags on your front inside, so they do not scrape the walls.
No flash inside. Phone photo rules: check at the ticket office.
Hawkers at the Colossi: a friendly 'no thank you' and keep walking.

kids.d: In each tomb, find a figure with the side-lock of youth. One point each, a bonus if he holds a fan.
In QV55 or QV44, count the gate guardians and their knives. Compare with whoever counted in the other tomb.
Explain to the adults what Egyptian blue is made of and why it counts as one of the first artificial colours. They must then find two blue things in the tomb.
At the Colossi, take one photo that makes someone in the family look tiny next to a throne. Best photo wins the front seat.

kids.t: Debate: close it or open it?
kids.d: Visitors' breath harms Nefertari's paintings. Should the tomb close forever and be shown only as a perfect copy? Teenagers take one side each.
In Tyti's tomb, find Hathor as a cow leaving a mountain. Back outside, point to that mountain.

glossary.d: Ancient name of the valley: place of beauty, or of the royal children.
Queens' Valley. The number is the order of recording.
'Amun is with his strong arm'. Son of Ramesses III, QV55.
'He who appears in Thebes'. Son of Ramesses III, QV44.
Queen, probably a wife of Ramesses III, QV52.
A braid over one ear, worn by children and some priests.
A metal rattle shaken in the worship of Hathor.
A board game of thirty squares; in tombs, a game against fate.

tonight: If a tomb were painted for you, who would walk in front of you, and what would be on the ceiling?
Ramesses III fills his sons' tombs. Love, or politics?
Giant statues or small painted figures: which will you remember better, and why?

sites.name: Medinet Habu
sites.kicker: Day 10 · west bank, temple of Ramesses III
sites.hook: A fortress-temple covered in carved battles, with more colour left on the walls than almost anywhere in Egypt.
facts: Colour on the ceilings and columns

story.title: The first strike in history
story.text: In the twenty-ninth year of Ramesses III, the workmen who cut and decorated the royal tombs went unpaid. Their rations of grain were late. They put their tools down, walked out to the temples near here, and sat down. A scribe wrote it all down on a papyrus. After some days, grain arrived. It is the first strike we have a written record of. The same king, who ruled a country under pressure from invaders, is shown on these walls winning every battle.

steps: The high gate, built like a Syrian fortress
First Pylon and the first court
Second Pylon and the second court: look up
Walk around the outside north wall: the battle with the Sea Peoples
Look back at the pylons from the garden

dont_miss.d: It is modelled on a fortified gate seen in Syria during Egyptian campaigns. Few Egyptian temples look like castles.
Blue skies, yellow stars, and vultures still shine in places. Imagine the whole temple like that.
A land battle and a sea battle against groups of raiders who attacked Egypt about 1177 BC. Ask the guide to show you the ships.
The reliefs are deeply sunk into the stone. In side light they cast shadows and read like drawings.

easy: In the second court, look for traces of a Christian church built among the temple columns in later centuries.
The temple had a small palace attached, with a Window of Appearances where the king showed himself.
Look for the line of royal statues standing as pillars, each in the form of the god of death and rebirth.
Count how many times the king is smiting enemies. Do the poses ever differ?
ask: What do we know about the Sea Peoples, and what remains uncertain?
How did the workmen's strike end?
How much of the original paint is left, and what keeps it alive?
Why is the temple so heavily fortified?
Why does Ramesses III copy Ramesses II so much?
quests: Look closer
Find a ceiling with colour. List every colour you can see. Which ones would have been the most expensive?
Debate
A relief shows a king winning every battle. How would you know if he really did? What would you want to check?
tips: The temple is wide and open. Walk the outside wall for the best battle reliefs.
Colours fade in sunlight. Photograph the ceilings in shade, with no flash.

deep.guide_line: A temple built like a castle, with real colour still on its ceilings and the oldest picture of a sea battle on its outside wall, and I will show you where each one is.

briefing.intro: Medinet Habu is the memorial temple of Ramesses III, built around 1180 BC, and the best-preserved temple of its kind on the west bank. It was a house for the king's spirit, where priests served him as a god after his death, and it was also a fortress, a palace, a treasury and later a whole town. Its walls carry more than seven thousand square metres of carved scenes, many still painted. The temple faces roughly east, towards the river, so we walk in a straight line from the morning side to the back: the fortified high gate, a small older temple beside it, the first pylon, two courts, then the ruined halls. Then we step outside to walk along the north wall, where the battles are, and finish on the south side at the palace and the hunting scene. Allow an hour and a half. The second court is the reward: look up there. The story of the workmen's strike under this king is in episode s12; here we look at the walls.

know.d: Ramesses III ruled about 1186 to 1155 BC. He admired Ramesses II and copied his memorial temple, the Ramesseum, almost room for room. Medinet Habu was built in one campaign, in roughly a dozen years, so it reads as a single design, which is rare in Egypt.

Most scenes are cut in sunk relief, the figures carved down into the wall, often very deep. Deep cuts survive weathering and are hard for a later king to erase. They also catch shadows: in side light the scenes jump out, in flat light they almost vanish.

Ceilings, column tops and the inner walls of the second court still carry blue, red, yellow and green paint. Part of it survived because later buildings, including a church, covered it for centuries. This is the best place on the trip to imagine how all temples once looked.

Ramesses III fought Libyans in the west and the Sea Peoples from the north. His temple got a mudbrick wall about 18 metres high and a gate shaped like a foreign fortress. In troubled centuries afterwards, the people of Thebes took refuge inside these walls.

know.t: The battles are on the outside
know.d: The north outer wall carries a long sequence of scenes: wars against the Libyans and the Sea Peoples, ending in the first known picture of a naval battle. They are big, clear and usually in shade. Many visitors skip them. Do not.

Small temples were added for fifteen hundred years. Later a Christian town called Djeme grew inside the walls, with a church in the second court. The town was abandoned around the 800s AD. The mudbrick walls you see around the edges are partly its houses.

Since 1924 the Epigraphic Survey of the University of Chicago has drawn every scene here to scale, line by line. Their volumes are one of the great records of Egyptology. If you see people on ladders with drawings, ask your guide; they may be at work.

numbers: about 18 m high, about 10 m thick
year 8 of the reign, about 1177 BC

tour.title: The high gate
tour.where: From the coach park, walk west towards the stone gate set in the outer wall. Stop in the open ground in front of it, facing west.
tour.look: Two towers with a passage between them and windows above: a gatehouse. Its shape copies the fortified gates, called migdol, that Egyptian armies met in Syria and Canaan. On the outer faces, the king smites enemies before the gods. Under the window ledges, look for carved heads of foreign captives, as if they held the windows up. Walk into the passage and look at the inner walls before you go through.
tour.story: The upper rooms of this gate are decorated with scenes of the king relaxing with young women of the palace, touching their chins, playing a board game. Some scholars read them as the harem; others as ritual images. Ramesses III died in a plot from his own harem: court records on a papyrus now in Turin describe the trials of the conspirators. In 2012 a CT scan of his mummy revealed a deep cut across his throat. The rooms are usually closed, so ask your guide.
spot: The smiting king on the outer faces
The slit windows of the upper rooms
tour.photo: Shoot the gate from 30 metres back, facing west, with people for scale; in the morning the sun is behind you and lights its face.
tour.ask: Are the upper rooms ever open, and what exactly is shown in them?

tour.title: Inside the gate: the older temples
tour.where: Through the gate, stop. Facing west towards the big pylon, the small temple of Amun is on your right (north), the chapels of the God's Wives on your left (south).
tour.look: The small temple on the right is older than everything else here: begun by Hatshepsut and completed by Thutmose III, about three hundred years before Ramesses III. Look for its pillars and the sanctuary walls with fine, shallow reliefs, a different hand from the deep Ramesside cutting. Its front was extended in much later times, up to the Romans. On the left, the stone chapels with doorways belong to the God's Wives of Amun, priestesses who ran the estate of Amun at Thebes around 750 to 525 BC.
tour.story: Why build here? This spot was believed to be one of the places where the world began, a mound that rose from the waters of creation, home of the eight first gods. Amun of Luxor was said to visit regularly to honour them. The God's Wives were royal daughters given to Amun, unmarried, very rich and politically powerful; each adopted her successor. Their chapels, among the last royal monuments of Thebes, show how long this ground stayed sacred.
spot: Shallow 18th-dynasty reliefs in the small temple
The doorway of a God's Wife chapel
Cartouches of Hatshepsut or Thutmose III
tour.ask: Which cartouches can we still see in the small temple, and were any of Hatshepsut's erased?

tour.title: The first pylon
tour.where: Continue west along the paved axis and stop 40 metres in front of the pylon, facing west.
tour.look: Sixty-three metres of wall, two towers, four vertical slots for flagpoles that once carried cedar masts with pennants. On each tower a giant Ramesses III grabs a bunch of enemies by the hair and raises his club before a god. Below run rows of oval name rings, each topped by a bound captive's head: the countries he claims to rule. Look at how deep the figures are cut: deep enough to fill with shadow.
tour.story: The pose of the king smiting enemies is three thousand years older than Ramesses III. It appears on the Narmer Palette around 3100 BC. Kings repeated it on every gateway because a pylon was a frontier between chaos outside and order inside. Some of the places in the lists here were copied from the monuments of Ramesses II, including lands Ramesses III probably never reached. So read the lists as a claim, then check the claim on the north wall later.
spot: Captive heads above the name rings
The god holding out the sword to the king
tour.photo: Late morning to midday, the sun swings to the south and skims across this east-facing wall: the deep carving reads best then.

tour.title: The first court
tour.where: Through the pylon gateway. Facing west: Osirid pillars on your right (north), a row of columns on your left (south), with an opening in the middle of the left wall.
tour.look: On the north side, square pillars fronted by statues of the king as Osiris, the god of rebirth, arms crossed. On the south side, papyrus columns and the facade of the palace. The opening in the middle is the Window of Appearances, where the king showed himself and handed gold collars to favoured officials. Look below and around the window for scenes of wrestlers and stick fighters, some of them foreigners, performing for the court.
tour.story: The palace behind that wall was a ceremonial residence: an audience hall, a throne room, a bathroom with a stone tank. Scholars are unsure whether the king ever slept here, or only came for festivals. The temple walls show the wars again, including a famous counting scene: scribes record enemy dead by tallying severed hands brought to them in heaps. Grim, and also the oldest kind of military bookkeeping.
tour.ask: Where exactly is the counting of hands, and why hands?

tour.title: The second court: look up
tour.where: Up the ramp and through the second pylon. Stop in the centre of the court, then walk to the shaded portico on the west side, facing west.
tour.look: Colour. Under the porticoes the walls, the bands under the ceiling and the column tops are still blue, red, yellow and green. The columns have closed papyrus-bud capitals with painted bands. Osirid pillars line the east and west sides. On the walls run the great festivals of Min and Sokar: priests carrying shrines, a white bull, standards. Stand in the shade of the west portico and look up at the ceiling band: vultures with spread wings, cartouches, stars.
tour.story: In Christian times, the people of Djeme built a church inside this court, the Holy Church of Djeme, with five aisles. They removed or hacked at some Osirid figures, and their mud plaster and later the town's debris covered the old paintings. Nineteenth-century excavators cleared the church away to reveal the temple. The protection it had given is a large part of why this court is the most colourful place you will see on the trip. Look for carved crosses on columns and doorjambs.
tour.photo: Stand in the shade, phone tilted up, tap the ceiling to expose for the colour and let the sky burn out.
tour.ask: How much of this colour is original, and has any been cleaned or restored?

tour.title: The back halls
