tour.where: Continue west through the doorway into the roofless area of column stumps, which runs to the back of the temple.
tour.look: This was the hypostyle hall, once roofed and dark, then smaller halls and the sanctuary at the far end, with side rooms all around. Only the lower parts stand now. Look for the side room of the treasury: it shows treasure, sacks of gold and precious objects piled up for Amun. Look at a column stump in section, built of drums, and at the floor where the roof lay. The light changes here: you leave the colour for bare sandstone.
tour.story: The king's body lay far away in the Valley of the Kings. This was where his statue received daily offerings, for millions of years in theory. Its estate owned fields, herds and workshops, and paid people. When the grain stopped arriving for the tomb workers, the strike in episode s12, these were the stores they had in mind. The roof slabs went into later building work.
spot: Where the sanctuary stood at the far west end

tour.title: The north wall: Sea Peoples
tour.where: Walk back out through the first court and leave the temple by the north side, then follow the outer north wall westwards, with the wall on your left.
tour.look: A long strip of battle. The Libyan campaigns, then the year 8 war against the Sea Peoples: on land, ox carts with women and children on the move, soldiers with round shields; and at sea, a tangle of ships. Egyptian ships have lion-head prows. Enemy ships have bird-head prows at both ends. Bodies fall into the water. Look at headgear: some enemies wear feathered crowns, others horned helmets. Between battles, the king hunts lions. This wall faces north and stays in shade most of the day.
tour.story: Around 1177 BC, cities around the eastern Mediterranean were destroyed and kingdoms such as the Hittites collapsed. Egyptian texts here say peoples from the islands came on together and no land could stand before them. Ramesses III claims he stopped them in the Nile mouths. Who they were is debated. The Peleset with feathered crowns are usually linked to the Philistines; others are harder to place. Drought, famine and migration all figure in modern theories.
tour.ask: Which group is which, and which identifications do scholars still argue about?

tour.title: The south side: palace and wild bulls
tour.where: Return to the first pylon and walk round to the south side of the temple, into the area of low mudbrick palace walls. Face east, towards the back (west face) of the pylon's southern tower.
tour.look: The low walls around you are the palace, partly rebuilt in modern brick so you can read the rooms. From here, find the back of the window you saw from the first court. Then look at the west face of the pylon's southern tower: the king in his chariot hunts wild bulls in a marsh. One bull collapses into the reeds, pierced. Below, soldiers and princes follow. Fish and birds fill the water and plants at the side.
tour.story: Royal hunts were ritual as much as sport: the king controlling wild nature as he controlled enemies. Many art historians count this bull hunt among the finest reliefs of its century, for its movement and the marsh life. Further along this south outer wall runs the festival calendar, about 1,470 lines listing every festival and its offerings. The palace and this wall get full sun, so come here last, and quickly.
spot: The dying bull in the reeds
Fish and birds in the marsh
The palace side of the Window of Appearances
tour.photo: Around midday the sun is high in the south and grazes the scene; shoot it straight on, filling the frame.

alone.intro: I leave you here for a while. The site is enclosed, the axis is straight, and you can always find your way back to the high gate. Use the time for what you liked most, and keep to the shade.

plans.d: Go back to the second court and sit in the west portico shade. Each person picks one column and finds every colour on it. Then walk to the first court and find the Window of Appearances and the wrestlers. Finish at the high gate, looking for the captive heads under the windows.

Do the north wall properly: from the first pylon westwards, find the ox carts, the lion hunt and the sea battle, and count the enemy ships. Then cross through the temple to the south side for the bull hunt, and back out through the small temple of Amun to compare its shallow reliefs with the deep Ramesside ones.
The north wall is in shade most of the day and the second court porticoes always have shade. Stay in those two places, drink, and skip the south side. Most of the colour is in the shade anyway.

alone.meet: Meet just inside the high gate, in its shadow, at the time your guide gives. It is the one exit everyone knows.

photos.where: In the high gate passage, facing west, framing the first pylon in the opening.
photos.when: Morning to midday, when the pylon is lit and the passage is dark.
photos.how: Tap the pylon to expose for it; the dark gate frames it. 1x or 0.5x if close.
photos.avoid: Groups standing in the passage; wait for a gap.

photos.where: In the west portico of the second court, in the shade, painted columns behind.
photos.when: Any time; the portico is shaded and light bounces softly off the court.
photos.how: Family in one row between two columns, photographer in the court facing west with the light behind. Tap the faces.
photos.avoid: Hard sun cutting across half the group; keep everyone fully inside the shade line.

photos.where: On the paved axis about 30 metres in front of the pylon, photographer further back to get the whole width.
photos.when: Late morning to midday, when the sun is high in the south and comes from the family's right side, out of their eyes.
photos.how: 0.5x wide, phone low, family small at the bottom, pylon filling the frame.
photos.avoid: The sun behind the pylon in the afternoon: everything goes dark.

photos.where: Under the second court portico or in a pylon gateway, looking straight up.
photos.when: Any time.
photos.how: Phone flat, pointing up, tap the brightest colour to expose. No flash.
photos.avoid: Including the bright sky at the edge, which flattens the colour.

photos.where: On the outer north wall, at the sea battle.
photos.when: Any time; the wall is in shade, so the light is soft and flat.
photos.how: Fill the frame with one ship. Lower the exposure a little to bring out the carving.
photos.avoid: Shooting at a steep angle from too close; step back.

photos.where: Beside an Osirid pillar on the north side of the first court.
photos.when: When that side is in shade.
photos.how: Portrait mode, subject a step in front of the pillar, face turned towards the open court for light.
photos.avoid: Standing in full sun with the pillar in shade.

photos.where: By the wrestling scene near the Window of Appearances.
photos.when: Any time.
photos.how: Two of the teenagers copy a wrestler pose beside the relief. Shoot side on.
photos.avoid: Touching the wall; keep a hand's width away.

photos.where: From the road or the café terraces east of the high gate, if your coach leaves that way.
photos.when: Afternoon light warms the gate from the west only on its back; morning is best for its front.
photos.how: Wide, with the mudbrick wall and the gate in one line.
photos.avoid: Parked coaches and wires.

details.d: The Peleset wear crowns that look like rows of feathers or reeds. They are often linked to the Philistines of the Bible.
Horned helmets mark the Sherden, who appear as enemies here and as soldiers in Egyptian service elsewhere.
Sea Peoples ships have bird heads at both ends, similar to boats painted on pottery from the Aegean world.
Ramesses III's throne name, Usermaatre-Meryamun, appears in cartouches everywhere. Look for the seated goddess Maat inside.
Put your eye near the edge of a sunk relief, without touching: some cuts go several centimetres into the stone.
Some blocks came from the destroyed memorial temple of Queen Tausret, a short-lived female ruler before Ramesses III.
Lion-head waterspouts on the roof edges took rare rain off the roof. Find one high on a wall.
Small crosses carved on columns and doorways are traces of the church and the town of Djeme.
Many Osirid statues lost faces or arms, some when the church was built, some to later stone hunters.
The south outer wall lists festivals day by day with their offerings: loaves, jars of beer, cattle.
The vertical grooves in the pylon held cedar poles brought from Lebanon, taller than the pylon.

qa.q: Why does it look like a castle?
qa.a: Partly display: the gate copies a foreign fortress, a trophy in architecture after Syrian campaigns. Partly real defence: the outer mudbrick wall was huge, and in later troubled times the people of Thebes sheltered inside it. Some scholars stress the symbolism more, some the security. Both are probably true.

qa.q: Who were the Sea Peoples?
qa.a: A modern name for groups the Egyptians list as Peleset, Tjeker, Shekelesh, Denyen, Weshesh and others, who attacked Egypt by land and sea around 1177 BC. Links to the Philistines, Sardinia or Sicily are proposed for some names, debated for others. Most historians see them as part of a wider crisis of drought, famine, migration and collapse across the eastern Mediterranean.

qa.q: Did Ramesses III really win?
qa.a: He kept Egypt intact while other kingdoms fell, so his claim of victory has some weight. But the texts are royal propaganda, the enemy lists borrow from older monuments, and the economy was strained enough that his tomb workers went on strike. Victory, yes, at a cost these walls do not show.

qa.q: How did Ramesses III die?
qa.a: Court records on papyrus describe a plot from inside the harem, aimed at putting a prince called Pentawer on the throne. A CT study of his mummy published in 2012 found a deep cut in the throat, and a later study found a toe injury. Whether he died during the attack is still discussed, but most scholars now think the plot killed him.

qa.q: Why is the colour still here?
qa.a: Shade, dry air, mineral pigments, and centuries under later buildings. The church in the second court and the town's houses covered walls and kept sun and wind off. Where the paint was exposed to sun and sand for three thousand years, it has gone.

qa.q: Why does it copy the Ramesseum?
qa.a: Ramesses II reigned for about 66 years and became the model of a great king. Ramesses III, a generation later and not his descendant in a direct line, took his style, his temple plan and even the names of his children. It was a way to claim the same success and legitimacy.

qa.q: What does 'Medinet Habu' mean?
qa.a: 'Medinet' is Arabic for town. The origin of 'Habu' is unknown. One idea links it to Amenhotep son of Hapu, a famous official whose temple stood nearby; another to an old name for the area. None explains the word fully.

qa.q: Did anyone live here after the pharaohs?
qa.a: Yes. A Christian town called Djeme filled the enclosure, with houses, streets and a church in the second court, until it was abandoned around the 800s AD. Many of the papyri and ostraca from that town survive and tell us about loans, wills and daily disputes.

practical: Allow about 1.5 hours. Your guide sets the order of the day.
Best order: gate, courts, north wall, then the sunny south side last.
The courts are open to the sky. Shade lies in the porticoes and along the north wall.
Hats and water: the paved approach and the south side are hot by late morning.
Flat walking on stone and dust; trainers are fine.
Toilets: usually near the entrance or in the cafés opposite. Check with your guide.
No flash on painted surfaces. Do not touch reliefs, even to point.
Guardians may offer to show you a 'secret' corner for a tip. Your choice; a polite no is fine.
There are cafés across from the entrance with shade and cold drinks for a break after.

kids.d: On the north wall, find a lion-head prow and a bird-head prow. Which side won?
In the second court, list every colour you can find on one column. Which was hardest to make?
Count how many times the king smites enemies on the gate and pylon. Do the poses ever change?
Explain why the carving is cut so deep. Two reasons. They must guess before you tell them.
The walls show victory, the strike papyrus shows hunger. Teenagers: which source would you trust, and why?
Sketch an Egyptian ship with its lion-head prow and sail. Put the date on it.

glossary.d: A fortified gate tower, a Semitic word. The high gate copies one.
The great twin-towered gateway of a temple.
A pillar fronted by a statue of the king as Osiris.
Carving cut into the wall surface, so figures sit below the surface.
Palace window where the king appeared and gave rewards.
One of the Sea Peoples, usually linked to the Philistines.
The Christian town that grew inside the walls.
A royal priestess who ran the god's estate at Thebes, about 750 to 525 BC.

tonight: If your house had walls covered in pictures of you, what would you show, and what would you leave out?
Was a temple-fortress a sign of strength or of fear?
The Sea Peoples are one of history's mysteries. What evidence would settle who they were?

sites.name: Temple of Hatshepsut
sites.hook: A temple of three terraces built against a cliff, built by a woman who ruled as king.
facts: about 1470 BC, Hatshepsut and her steward Senenmut

story.title: A queen with a king's beard
story.text: Hatshepsut began as the regent for a young stepson, Thutmose III. Within a few years she had herself crowned king and was shown in statues with the royal beard, kilt and crown. She ruled for about twenty years, and during that time trade flourished, and the temple at Deir el-Bahari was built. Later, many of her images were hacked out and her statues smashed. Historians still argue who did it, and why. The temple outlived her attackers.

steps: From the car park: the whole temple against the cliff
Lower terrace: Osiride statues
Middle terrace, south: Punt reliefs and the Hathor chapel
Middle terrace, north: the divine birth reliefs and Anubis chapel
Upper terrace: the sun court (check access)
Look back: the axis points across the river to Karnak

dont_miss.d: Five ships sail to a faraway land for incense trees, gold, ebony, animals. The ships are carved in detail.
A small chapel on the north side with the best colour: painted gods in a jewel-box room.
The temple is a calm series of terraces. It copies the curved cliff behind it.
In several scenes the queen's figure was cut out. See the scars on the stone.

easy: Next to the temple, to the south, lie the ruins of an older temple of Mentuhotep II. Hatshepsut copied that idea.
Look at the Punt scenes for the large queen of Punt and the donkey that carries her. The artists enjoyed the details.
The temple axis points across the river to Karnak's sanctuary.
Hatshepsut planted incense trees brought back from Punt. Ask the guide to point out the tree pits.
ask: Who defaced Hatshepsut's images, and when?
Where was Punt, and how do we know?
How did the builders get stone up the cliff?
Who was Senenmut, and is there a tomb or a portrait?
What is the difference between this and a tomb?
quests: Look closer
Find a scene with a ship. Count the oars, sails and cargo. What would you carry home from a far land?
Debate
If a ruler is so successful, why would people erase her name after she died? Give three possible reasons.
tips: The temple is on a wide open slope. Hat, water, sun cream.
Stairs and ramps. The upper terrace may be closed, so ask before you climb.

deep.guide_line: I walk you up the three terraces in the right order, show you the carvings that matter, and tell you where to stand for the family photo everyone wants here.

briefing.intro: The coach stops at a visitor centre with a bazaar, a small electric tram takes you most of the way, and then the whole temple is in front of you: three terraces stacked against a curved limestone cliff, joined by two long ramps on one central line. Its ancient name was Djeser-Djeseru, the holiest of holy places. It was built for the god Amun and for the memory of Hatshepsut, who ruled as king from about 1479 to 1458 BC. It was never her tomb: that lies in the Valley of the Kings, behind the cliff. Once a year the statue of Amun crossed the river from Karnak, came up the causeway and spent a night here. Our route is simple. Up the axis, then the middle terrace one wing at a time (Punt and Hathor to the south, the birth story and Anubis to the north), up to the top court, and a last look back towards Karnak. Her life story is in episode l06. Today is about reading the walls.

know.d: The temple faces east-southeast, towards the river and Karnak. Looking up the ramp you face roughly west, so south is on your left and north on your right. Punt and the Hathor chapel are on the left, the birth reliefs and the Anubis chapel on the right, and the ruin of Mentuhotep II further left again.

In the Beautiful Festival of the Valley, Amun's boat-shrine left Karnak, crossed the Nile and came up a causeway about one kilometre long, lined with more than a hundred sphinxes, to spend a night in the sanctuary. West bank families visited their dead at the same time, with food and music.

A Polish mission has worked here since 1961, reassembling fallen blocks and filling gaps with new stone. The rule is easy: carved or stained stone is old, pale smooth stone is modern. The restorers kept the difference visible on purpose.

In scene after scene a figure has been chiselled away, leaving a rough silhouette. That was usually Hatshepsut. Sometimes her names were recut as those of Thutmose I, II or III. After two or three you will spot them everywhere. Who did it, and why, is in episode l06.

Most carving here is raised relief: the background was cut away so figures stand up a few millimetres. In flat shade it disappears. Look along the wall at a low angle, or hold a phone torch low and sideways. Never shine it into faces or onto paint for long.

Hatshepsut chose this bay because Mentuhotep II, who reunited Egypt around 2050 BC, had built a terraced temple here five centuries earlier. Between the two, higher up, Thutmose III later added a third temple. A rockfall destroyed it in antiquity.

Deir el-Bahari means "the monastery of the north". From about the sixth century AD, Christian monks of Saint Phoibammon lived on the upper terrace, painted over some reliefs and left crosses. Excavators removed the monastery, but traces remain.

The middle and upper terraces are usually open. Inner rooms (the Hathor halls, the solar court, the sanctuary) open and close with restoration work. Ask your guide on arrival what is open today, before anyone climbs in the heat.

numbers: 5 ships, about year 9 of the reign

tour.title: The approach: the whole temple at once
tour.where: Get off the tram, walk forward onto the line of the ramps and face the cliff.
tour.look: Read it as one drawing: two lines of square pillars, two ramps on one axis, the cliff curving behind like a stage set. The terraces get shallower as they rise, which makes the building look taller. On the lower court, near the foot of the first ramp, look for round pits cut in the rock and one old tree stump behind a low wall. To the left, lower and browner, is Mentuhotep's ruin.
tour.story: People say the temple looks modern. The front was largely rebuilt in the twentieth century, so the edges are crisp, but the idea is ancient and borrowed from Mentuhotep next door. The lower court was a garden: the Punt reliefs say living incense trees were brought back in baskets and planted for Amun. The stump is usually called one of them. Scholars are more careful: some pits may have held persea trees, also sacred.
spot: The two ramps on one line
Tree pits and the walled stump
tour.photo: The classic wide view: 0.5x, walk back until the cliff top fits, wait for a gap on the ramp.

tour.title: The lower porticoes: obelisks and a sphinx
tour.where: Before climbing, step into the shade of the lower colonnade left (south) of the ramp, then cross to the right (north) one.
tour.look: On the south back wall, low down, find a long barge carrying two obelisks laid end to end, towed by rows of smaller boats. On the north side, hunting and fishing scenes and Hatshepsut as a sphinx trampling enemies. Both are worn. You need patience and side light.
tour.story: The barge is a building report: the transport of two obelisks from Aswan to Karnak. You saw one of Hatshepsut's obelisks standing at Karnak on day 5, about 30 m in one piece. Here is how it travelled. The sphinx says the usual royal message: the king keeps chaos away. Engineering on one side, ideology on the other, at the front door.
tour.ask: Can you show us the obelisk barge?

tour.title: The Punt colonnade
tour.where: Up the first ramp to the middle terrace, then left (south) along the back wall.
tour.look: Read it like a comic strip. Ships with big sails and rows of oars over a sea full of fish. Houses on stilts with ladders, under palms. The chief of Punt, his large wife and her donkey. Then the loading: sacks, trees in baskets, baboons, and the cargo weighed for Amun. The fish are precise enough for zoologists to name Red Sea species.
tour.story: Episode l06 tells the voyage. What it does not say: at Mersa Gawasis on the Red Sea coast, archaeologists in the 2000s found caves with ropes, cedar ship timbers, cargo boxes and texts about Punt. So the ships were probably carried in pieces across the desert, assembled on the coast and sailed south. One more thing: the panel of the queen of Punt is widely reported to be a cast, with the original block in Cairo.
spot: A stilt house and its ladder
The queen of Punt and the donkey
tour.photo: Shoot at a slight angle so the light rakes across the carving. No flash.

tour.title: The Hathor chapel
tour.where: Keep going south to the end of the middle terrace, to the columns with women's faces.
tour.look: Each capital is Hathor's face, a woman with cow's ears, set on the shape of a sistrum, the rattle played for her. Some faces were hacked off, others survive. Inside, when open, are halls with reliefs, including the young queen drinking milk from Hathor in her cow form.
tour.story: Hathor was goddess of music and joy, and here also mistress of the western cliff, whose cow came out of the mountain to welcome the dead. A chapel to her at the foot of this cliff is a natural choice. Senenmut's hidden portraits (episode l06) were cut in niches in this chapel and the upper sanctuary. Ask whether one is visible today.
spot: A smashed face beside an intact one

tour.title: The birth colonnade
tour.where: Walk back past the foot of the upper ramp into the right (north) half of the middle colonnade.
tour.look: Calm, formal scenes in pale paint. Find Amun seated face to face with a queen, knees touching, held up by two goddesses: conception, told with discretion. Then the ram-headed god Khnum at a potter's wheel shaping two small identical figures. Then birth, nursing, and presentation to Amun.
tour.story: This is the oldest known full divine birth cycle, later copied by Amenhotep III at Luxor Temple. The argument is political: the ruler is Amun's own child. The detail most people miss is the second figure on the wheel. It is the child's ka, the life force made with every person, which needs offerings after death. Feeding that ka is one of the jobs of this temple.
spot: Touching knees of Amun and the queen
Child and ka, side by side

tour.title: The Anubis chapel
tour.where: At the north end of the middle terrace, a small porch of columns leads in.
tour.look: The best colour on the site. Jackal-headed Anubis on a throne, offerings heaped in front of him: loaves, meat, ducks, lotus, jars. A blue ceiling with yellow stars. Look for a blank outline where Hatshepsut stood before a god, and, nearby, Thutmose III untouched. The two together tell the whole story of the erasure.
tour.story: Colour survives because the room is roofed and sun never reached it. The pigments are minerals: ochres for red and yellow, gypsum white, soot black, and Egyptian blue, a man-made copper glass and one of the first synthetic pigments. Anubis, god of embalming and guardian of the cemetery, is the right host for a temple of the afterlife.
tour.photo: Low light: elbows tucked, breathe out, let night mode work. No flash.

tour.title: The upper ramp and the Osiride portico
tour.where: Climb the central upper ramp. The row of tall statues with crossed arms faces you at the top.
tour.look: Twenty-six pillars, each fronted by Hatshepsut as Osiris: wrapped body, arms crossed, crook and flail, a beard and a red-brown face, the colour used for men. Many are rebuilt from pieces. Compare faces: ancient ones keep paint and eye lines, modern ones are plain. Look for the falcon at the top of the ramp balustrade.
tour.story: The Osiris form says the king joins the god of rebirth after death. The male skin colour was part of the king's costume, like the beard, not a claim about her body. Statues of her that the Metropolitan Museum pieced together in the 1920s from dumps nearby are now in New York and Cairo.
tour.photo: Portrait: one person beside a pillar, in the shade line, not touching it. Portrait mode, tap the face.

tour.title: The upper court, the sanctuary and the view back
tour.where: Through the granite doorway into the upper court; the sanctuary is cut into the cliff straight ahead. Come back out to the top of the ramp afterwards.
tour.look: The court was ringed with pillars and carved with festival boats, priests and musicians. In the back wall, rows of niches held statues. Ahead, the sanctuary enters the rock. Right (north): the solar court with a stepped sun altar. Left (south): offering chapels for Hatshepsut and her father Thutmose I. Then, outside, turn round: the axis runs down the ramps and across the plain towards the river and Karnak, about five kilometres away.
tour.story: Amun's boat spent its festival night in the sanctuary. Under the Ptolemies the inner room became a healing shrine to two deified wise men, Imhotep and Amenhotep son of Hapu, and pilgrims left Greek graffiti. Many say the axis catches the winter-solstice sunrise. A 2019 study found it close but not exact. The link to Karnak is certain.
spot: Statue niches in the back wall
The axis line across the plain
tour.ask: Which inner rooms are open today?

tour.title: Mentuhotep II and the royal cache
tour.where: Back on the lower court, walk to its south edge and look over the older ruin.
tour.look: A low platform, pillar stumps, and the base of a square central block. Some reconstructions put a pyramid or mound on it, others a flat roof; scholars still argue. It is five centuries older than Hatshepsut's temple and hard to read, which is why two minutes here pay off.
tour.story: Mentuhotep II reunited Egypt around 2050 BC. In 1900 Howard Carter's horse stumbled into a hole in front of this temple, which led to a passage and a seated statue of the king painted black, now in Cairo. In the cliffs a little south of here, a village family found a shaft in the 1870s holding the mummies of great kings, Seti I and Ramesses II among them, hidden by priests. Officials cleared it in 1881.
spot: The southern cliffs of the royal cache
tour.ask: Where exactly was the royal cache?

alone.intro: Here I leave you. The site is one axis with the bazaar behind you, so nobody gets lost. Pick one plan. Shade exists only under the porticoes. Keep the younger ones close on the ramps.

plans.d: Go straight to the middle terrace. Ten minutes in the Punt colonnade on the south side: fish, stilt houses, the queen of Punt. Then cross to the Anubis chapel at the north end for the colour. Come down the central ramp and take one wide photo from the forecourt.

Start at the top while you have energy: Osiride portico, upper court, the solar altar if open. Down to the middle terrace: Hathor at the far south end, then Punt, then the birth colonnade and Anubis at the north end. Finish at the south edge of the lower court above Mentuhotep's ruin.

Skip the top. Stay inside the middle colonnades, which keep shade most of the day. Sit on a modern step, drink, and do one mission from the kids list. The tram back is short and the visitor centre has cold drinks.

plans.t: If you want one more thing
plans.d: A graffiti hunt: Coptic crosses and Greek letters on the upper terrace, travellers' names from the 1800s. Then find an erased figure with a recut cartouche and work out whose name replaced hers.

alone.meet: Meet at the foot of the lower ramp by the walled tree stump at the agreed time. Anyone waiting stands in the shade of the lower south portico.

photos.where: Forecourt, on the axis, about 40 to 60 m back from the first ramp.
photos.when: Best in the morning, sun behind the photographer. After about 1 pm the façade is in shade and the sun hangs over the cliff to the south-west.
photos.how: Six in a tight line in the lower third, slightly off-centre so the ramp shows. Chest height, 0.5x if needed. Afternoon: tap a face to expose for the shade.
photos.avoid: The tram and the ramp crowd behind your heads, sun flare from the upper left.

photos.t: The view back to the river
photos.where: Upper terrace, beside (not on) the top of the upper ramp, facing east.
photos.when: Midday and afternoon, when the plain is lit.
photos.how: Ramps on a diagonal into green fields. For a family version, everyone at one side, turned three-quarters so nobody squints.
photos.avoid: Guards at the ramp top, a horizon through heads.

photos.where: Upper portico, a pillar near either end of the row.
photos.when: Any time; the portico gives shade from late morning.
photos.how: Stand beside the statue looking up at it. Portrait mode at the person's eye height, tap the face.
photos.avoid: Touching the statue; tourists behind: step sideways until a pillar hides them.

photos.where: Hathor columns, south end of the middle terrace.
photos.when: Late morning to early afternoon, face lit from the south.
photos.how: Crouch close, aim up, fill a vertical frame with face and cow ears on blue. 1x or 2x, never wide.
photos.avoid: The sun right behind the capital.

photos.where: Inside the Anubis chapel.
photos.when: Any time; dim inside.
photos.how: Stand at an angle to the wall to avoid glare, brace, fill the frame with Anubis and the offerings.
photos.avoid: Flash, backs in the doorway.

photos.where: Upper terrace in front of the portico, clear of the doorway.
photos.when: When a gap opens: thirty seconds is enough.
photos.how: Everyone in a row, arms crossed on the chest, chin up, straight face; shoot from slightly low. Then a take where everyone laughs.
photos.avoid: Blocking the ramp, posing on ancient stone.

photos.where: South edge of the lower court, looking north-west: Mentuhotep's ruin in front, Hatshepsut's colonnades behind.
photos.when: Midday is fine.
photos.how: 0.5x, ruin across the bottom, horizon in the top third.
photos.avoid: The fence and path along the edge.

photos.where: From the forecourt or the coach road.
photos.when: Only early: the cliff faces east and glows gold in the morning, then goes flat.
photos.how: Cliff fills the frame, temple small and low: it shows the scale.
photos.avoid: Hoping for sunset here: by late afternoon the sun is behind the cliff.

details.d: Where her name was erased, another king's was carved in the same oval. The recut edges look rougher or deeper.
Ancient faces keep red-brown paint and black eye lines. The modern replacements beside them are plain.
In the Punt scenes specialists recognise pufferfish, rays and a turtle among other sea life.
Baboons ride in the Punt cargo. A 2020 study of mummified baboons supports a Punt around Eritrea and Ethiopia.
Monks lived here from about the sixth century. Look for small crosses and Coptic letters on the upper walls.
Where both rulers appear, his figure is often intact beside her empty outline. The erasure was selective.
Part of the north side of the middle terrace was never decorated. Work stopped and nobody came back.
His tomb near the forecourt has the oldest known painted astronomical ceiling. Usually closed: ask.
High between the two big temples, his temple Djeser-Akhet was crushed by a rockfall. Painted fragments were found from 1962.
Ties, nets and walls protect against rockfalls. That is why some paths are closed.
The barge in the lower south portico carries two obelisks end to end. Count the towing boats: it took a fleet to move it.

qa.q: Was Hatshepsut buried here?
qa.a: No. This was her temple of offerings and memory. Her tomb, KV20, is in the Valley of the Kings behind the cliff, a corridor of about two hundred metres curving down. Some scholars think it was aimed towards this temple so the burial would lie beneath it, but bad rock stopped it. Attractive, unproven, and KV20 is not open.

qa.q: How did they build terraces against a cliff?
qa.a: Mostly built, not carved. Retaining walls of limestone blocks were filled behind with rubble and faced with fine stone. Earth and brick ramps lifted blocks, and the central ramps doubled as the procession route. Only the sanctuary and some chapels are cut into the rock.

qa.q: How much is original?
qa.a: The lower and middle colonnades stand on ancient foundations with many original blocks. The upper portico and many Osiride statues were rebuilt from fragments with new stone where pieces were missing. Pale, smooth and uncarved means modern; carved or stained means ancient.

qa.q: Why are some Hathor faces smashed?
qa.a: Several causes. Hatshepsut's attackers targeted her, not goddesses. Later some Christians defaced pagan faces. Earthquakes, rockfalls and stone robbers did the rest. A neat chisel removal of a face is probably deliberate; a whole broken block is more likely nature.

qa.q: How did the expedition reach Punt?
qa.a: Probably by sea from the Red Sea coast. At Mersa Gawasis, east of the Nile bend, excavators found ship timbers, ropes, cargo boxes and texts naming Punt. Ships were likely carried in pieces from the Nile, assembled on the coast, sailed south, and the cargo hauled back overland. Punt's exact location is still debated.

qa.q: Who was Mentuhotep II?
qa.a: A Theban ruler who reunited Egypt around 2050 BC and began the Middle Kingdom. To later Thebans he was a founding hero. Building next to him tied Hatshepsut to a respected ancestor, useful for a ruler in an unusual position, and it gave her the finest natural setting on the west bank.

qa.q: Do we know who the architect was?
qa.a: The best candidate is Senenmut, her steward, who held titles over royal works and placed his own image in hidden niches here. No text says plainly that he designed it, and the high priest Hapuseneb also oversaw works. Most scholars credit Senenmut with a leading role and stay careful with the word architect.

qa.q: Can we walk from here to the Valley of the Kings?
qa.a: An old workmen's path crosses the cliff, and visitors used to hike it. Access has been restricted at times, and it is hot and exposed. By road it is a short drive round the hills. If the family adds the Valley of the Kings, ask the representative and your guide; do not try the path alone.

practical: About 1.5 h on site, plus 15 minutes for the bazaar and tram.
The tram has a small separate fee; check on the day. Walking is long and shadeless.
Shade only under the colonnades. Late October afternoons are often in the low thirties.
One litre of water each, hats, sun cream. Cold drinks at the visitor centre.
Toilets are at the visitor centre, not in the temple.
Shoes with grip: ramps are smooth and dusty.
No flash, no drones. Phone photos are normally fine; check if any camera ticket applies.
The bazaar is persistent. One person speaks, the rest keep walking.
Decline guardians who offer closed rooms for a tip, or ask your guide first.
If this comes last in the day, do the 20-minute plan with the younger ones.

kids.d: In the Punt colonnade, find five different sea creatures under the ships. Draw the strangest one.
On the upper portico, count ancient faces against modern ones. Report the score.
Draw a Punt house on stilts with its ladder, then explain why you would build one.
Find an erased figure and a nearby cartouche. Hers, or recut? Check with the guide, then teach the method to your parents.
Should missing statue parts be rebuilt in new stone, or left as ruins? One minute each side.
Find Khnum's wheel with two children on it and explain what a ka is and why a temple feeds it.

glossary.d: Female king of the 18th Dynasty, about 1479 to 1458 BC.
The monastery of the north: Arabic name of the bay.
The temple's name: holiest of holy places.
Reunified Egypt about 2050 BC; built the older temple next door.
Hatshepsut's steward and probable master builder.
Land of incense reached by sea, probably the southern Red Sea region.
The king as Osiris: wrapped body, crossed arms, crook and flail.
The life force made with each person, fed with offerings after death.

tonight: If you could send one expedition to bring back a wonder for your home town, where would it go?
Did the rebuilt statues make the temple better, or less true?
Hatshepsut used a story of divine birth to justify her rule. What stories do leaders use today?

sites.name: Valley of the Kings (optional)
sites.kicker: Day 10 · west bank · optional, not in the printed programme
sites.hook: The dry valley behind the cliff where Egypt's kings were buried for about 450 years, in painted tombs cut deep into the rock.
facts: about 2 to 2.5 h, if added (ask the representative)
Ceilings of stars and the sky goddess Nut

story.title: The tomb that hid under the workmen's huts
story.text: Some 180 years after Tutankhamun was buried, workmen cut a large tomb for Ramesses V and VI just above and west of his small one. They built stone huts to live in while they worked, right on top of the rubble that covered the boy king's stairs. Robbers who emptied almost every other tomb in the valley never found the way in. In 1922 Howard Carter cleared those huts and found the first step. The workmen's mess saved the best-preserved royal burial ever found.

steps: Optional: confirm with the representative before the day, and check tickets
Visitor centre: the model of the valley, and buy any extra tomb tickets here
The electric tram to the valley floor
Three tombs on the general ticket, chosen from those open today
Extra tickets if you want them: Tutankhamun, Ramesses VI, Seti I (check)
Look up at el-Qurn, the pyramid-shaped peak above the valley

dont_miss.d: Burial chamber ceilings show the sky goddess Nut or star tables. Ramesses VI (KV9) has the most famous one, on a separate ticket.

dont_miss.t: The sun disc over the door
dont_miss.d: Above many tomb entrances, a disc holds a scarab and a ram-headed god: the sun at dawn and at night. It tells you what the tomb is about.
His mummy lies in a glass case in the antechamber of KV62, the only object of his tomb that most visitors will see in Luxor.
Feel the slope as you walk down. The sun god went down the same way every night.

easy: Tomb numbers (KV2, KV62) mostly follow the order in which tombs were recorded, so KV62 was the sixty-second.
Ramesses III's tomb has a side room with two blind harpists, which is why travellers called it the Tomb of the Harpers.
In 2025 Egypt announced that a tomb found in a side valley in 2022 belonged to Thutmose II, Hatshepsut's husband: the first royal tomb identified since Tutankhamun's.
Greek and Roman tourists visited some tombs. Look for their scratched names near the entrances of KV2 and KV9.
ask: Which tombs are open today, and which three do you recommend for our family?
Can we buy the Tutankhamun or Ramesses VI ticket here, and is phone photography allowed inside?
How did the workmen get here every day from their village?
Why did the kings stop building pyramids and hide their tombs here?
What does the Book of Gates show, and how do we read it on the wall?
quests: Look closer
In one tomb, find the sun in three forms: a scarab beetle, a disc and a ram-headed man. Which time of day does each one mean?
Debate
Tutankhamun's mummy stays in his tomb while all his treasure went to Cairo. Is that the right choice? Two reasons each way.
tips: OPTIONAL ADD-ON: the Valley of the Kings is not in your printed programme. Ask the representative early whether it can be added on day 10, at what cost, and what it replaces.
Tickets, open tombs and photo rules change often. Buy extra tomb tickets at the main ticket office before the tram: you usually cannot buy them at the tombs. No flash, ever.
The valley is a shadeless limestone bowl. Go as early as possible, carry water, and rest inside the visitor centre, not on the valley floor.

deep.guide_line: If you add the valley, I show you how to choose your three tombs, how to read a royal tomb from the door to the burial chamber, and how to survive the heat.

briefing.intro: First, a flag: the Valley of the Kings is not in your printed programme. If the family wants it, ask the representative early whether it can be added on day 10, at what cost, and what it replaces. If it happens, here is the shape of the visit. The coach stops at a visitor centre with a big model of the valley and the ticket office. A small electric tram runs up to the valley floor. Then you are in a dry limestone gorge with little doorways cut into its sides, each with a number: KV for Kings' Valley. For about 450 years, from roughly 1500 to 1070 BC, the kings of the New Kingdom were buried here, hidden behind the cliff from Hatshepsut's temple. A general ticket lets you into three of the tombs open that day. Your guide explains outside each entrance, because talking inside is usually not allowed. So listen at the door, then go in and look. The Tutankhamun story is in episode l01. This page is about how to visit.

know.d: The general ticket covers three tombs from a rotating list of those open that day. A few tombs need their own extra ticket, usually Tutankhamun (KV62), Ramesses VI (KV9) and Seti I (KV17), which is by far the most expensive. Buy extras at the main ticket office before the tram. Prices and rules change: check on the day.

Pyramids were obvious targets for robbers. From the early New Kingdom, kings cut their tombs in this hidden valley instead, and built their temples for worship separately, on the edge of the fields: Hatshepsut's, Medinet Habu. Above the valley rises el-Qurn, a natural pyramid-shaped peak. Many think that helped the choice.

know.t: The shape of a royal tomb
know.d: A stair, then a series of sloping corridors going down, sometimes a deep shaft, a pillared hall, more corridors, and finally the burial chamber, which the Egyptians called the House of Gold. Early tombs turn corners; later ones, from about 1300 BC, run straight into the hill and get wider and higher.

know.t: The walls are a guidebook to the night
know.d: The decoration is mostly a set of funerary books describing the sun's journey through the twelve hours of night and its rebirth at dawn. The king hoped to travel with the sun. Read the walls as a map: you walk down into the night, the sun comes back up at the end.

The Amduat, "what is in the underworld", shows the sun boat travelling through twelve hours, in three bands of figures. The Book of Gates divides the night by twelve gates, each guarded by a serpent. Both show the dead, the good and the punished. Spot the snakes standing on their tails at each gate.

Corridor ceilings often carry flying vultures and rows of yellow stars. Burial chamber ceilings show the sky goddess Nut, her body arched across the room, swallowing the sun at evening and giving birth to it at morning, or tables of star groups.

Rules have changed several times in recent years. Sometimes phone photos inside are included, sometimes a photo ticket is needed, sometimes photography is banned in particular tombs. Ask at the ticket office. Flash is always forbidden: it damages the paint.

The tombs were cut and painted by a team of skilled workmen living in a village over the hill, Deir el-Medina. They walked to work across the cliff on a path you can still see. Their strike under Ramesses III is episode s12.

numbers: 12, in the Amduat and the Book of Gates

tour.title: The visitor centre and the model
tour.where: Inside the visitor centre next to the coach park, before the tram.
tour.look: A large model of the valley shows the tombs as cut-away tunnels under the hills. Find the long straight tombs of the Ramesside kings and the small, cramped Tutankhamun. Note how close many are: some tomb diggers broke into an older tomb by accident. There is often a short film about Carter's discovery.
tour.story: Two minutes here make the rest of the visit readable. Underground, the valley is a tangle of tunnels, and the model shows the plan that no one ever sees from the surface. This is also where decisions are made. Ask your guide which tombs are open today and choose your three before the tram. Extra tickets are sold here, not at the tombs.
tour.ask: Which three of today's open tombs would you choose for a family with children?

tour.title: The tram and the valley floor
tour.where: Take the small electric tram up to the valley entrance, then walk in along the main path.
tour.look: A gorge of pale limestone with no plant in sight, scattered rocks, low walls and paths, and a doorway every few dozen metres with a sign and a number. Look up at the pyramid-shaped peak above the valley: el-Qurn, the horn. Wooden shelters near the tombs give a little shade.
tour.story: The valley floods rarely, but violently. Flash floods filled many tombs with debris over the centuries, which damaged paintings and also hid entrances. A goddess was thought to live on the peak: Meretseger, "she who loves silence", a cobra who protected the necropolis and punished workmen who broke the rules.
tour.photo: Family photo on the main path with el-Qurn behind: see the photo spots.

tour.title: Reading a tomb from the door
tour.where: At the entrance of your first tomb, before you go down.
tour.look: Above the doorway, look for a yellow disc. Inside it, a scarab beetle and a ram-headed man, often with the goddesses Isis and Nephthys kneeling on each side. On the first walls inside, look for the king before the falcon-headed sun god, and long lists of the sun's names. Then the slope begins, with handrails and wooden walkways.
tour.story: The disc says it all: the scarab is the sun at dawn, the ram-headed man the sun at night. The tomb is a machine for joining that cycle. The first texts are often the Litany of Ra, a list of the sun god's many forms. Keep your bearings by the books: if you see boats and snakes in three bands, it is the Amduat; snakes guarding doorways mean the Book of Gates.
spot: The disc with scarab and ram
The king meeting the sun god
tour.ask: Which book is on this wall, and which hour of the night?

tour.title: Ramesses IV, KV2
tour.where: Usually one of the first tombs on the main path near the entrance; check if it is open.
tour.look: A straight, wide tomb about 89 m long. Near the entrance, Greek and Coptic graffiti: names and crosses scratched by ancient visitors and monks who lived inside. At the end, a huge broken granite sarcophagus still stands in the burial chamber, under a ceiling with the sky goddess Nut and star tables.
tour.story: Ramesses IV's tomb is famous for a document: a plan of it drawn on papyrus, now in Turin, showing the sarcophagus surrounded by nested shrines like Tutankhamun's. It is one of the oldest architectural drawings known. The tomb was open in antiquity, and Greek and Roman tourists left hundreds of graffiti. You are not the first tourist here by two thousand years.

tour.title: Ramesses IX, KV6
tour.where: Close to the entrance area too, with an unusually wide doorway.
tour.look: Bright, broad corridors with crowded walls of figures, many in yellow and red. In the burial chamber, the vaulted ceiling shows Nut stretched across the room, and the walls carry the Book of Caverns and the Book of the Earth, with gods lifting the sun out of the ground.
tour.story: This tomb shows a reign cut short. Side rooms off the first corridor were begun but never finished, and the pillared hall was not completed. The workmen raced to finish what mattered: the burial chamber. Roman and Coptic visitors also left graffiti here.

tour.title: Ramesses III, KV11
tour.where: On the main path in the central part of the valley.
tour.look: A long tomb, about 188 m, with small side rooms off the first corridors. In them, unusual scenes: storerooms, weapons, boats, Nile gods, and the famous two blind harpists singing to the gods. Then watch the corridor: at one point the axis jogs sideways.
tour.story: The tomb was begun by Setnakhte, Ramesses III's father, whose workmen broke into the older tomb of Amenmesse next door by mistake. They gave up. Ramesses III restarted it, shifting the line to miss his neighbour. James Bruce described it in 1768, and his drawing of the harpists made it the Tomb of the Harpers. The sarcophagus box is now in the Louvre and its lid in Cambridge.
spot: The sideways jog in the corridor
Weapons and boats in the side rooms
tour.ask: Where exactly did the workmen break into the next tomb?

tour.title: Merenptah, KV8
tour.where: On a side branch of the valley; a steep walk down.
tour.look: A very long, steep descent, about 160 m of corridors, with carved relief rather than paint in many places. In the burial chamber, a huge granite sarcophagus lid with the king carved on top as Osiris, arms crossed.
tour.story: Merenptah was the thirteenth son of Ramesses II and became king as an old man, because his father lived so long. He is famous for a victory stela that contains the oldest known mention of the name Israel. His sarcophagi were so big that the doorjambs had to be cut and rebuilt to get them in. Later, his mummy was moved to the royal cache at Deir el-Bahari.
spot: The king's face on the lid

tour.title: Ramesses VI, KV9 (extra ticket)
tour.where: In the centre of the valley, just above the entrance to Tutankhamun's tomb.
tour.look: If you buy one extra ticket, many people say this is the one. The burial chamber ceiling shows Nut twice, back to back, stretched across the vault in blue and gold, with the Book of the Day and the Book of the Night: the sun travelling through her body. The corridors are decorated from end to end.
tour.story: The tomb was begun for Ramesses V and taken over by Ramesses VI. Greek and Roman visitors called it the tomb of Memnon and covered the entrance with graffiti. The rubble from its digging, and the workmen's huts built on it, covered the entrance of Tutankhamun's tomb below. That accident probably saved the boy king from the robbers.
tour.photo: If photos are allowed: 0.5x, phone flat, pointed straight up from the centre of the room.

tour.title: Tutankhamun, KV62 (extra ticket)
tour.where: Low in the valley floor, below KV9. Sixteen steps down, a short corridor.
tour.look: Small and simple. In the antechamber, his mummy lies in a climate-controlled glass case, face and feet visible, the rest covered in linen. In the burial chamber, the quartzite sarcophagus and the only painted walls: twelve baboons from the first hour of the Amduat, the funeral procession, and Ay, his successor, performing the Opening of the Mouth.
tour.story: The treasures, more than five thousand objects, are in the Grand Egyptian Museum you saw on day 2. The gilded outer coffin that stayed here for decades was taken to the museum for restoration in 2019. Ask your guide what is inside the sarcophagus today. The tomb was probably cut for someone less important and adapted after his early death: the walls look rushed. From 2009 to 2019 the Getty Conservation Institute worked here with Egypt to protect the paintings from visitors' breath and dust.
spot: Twelve baboons on the west wall
Ay in the leopard skin of a priest
tour.ask: What is inside the sarcophagus now?

tour.title: Seti I, KV17 (if open, extra ticket)
tour.where: Ask first: it is often closed or on the most expensive ticket.
tour.look: Often called the finest tomb in Egypt, about 137 m long, decorated almost everywhere with fine raised relief and bright paint: the Litany of Ra, the Amduat, the Book of Gates, and an astronomical ceiling in the burial chamber. Some walls have gaps where panels were cut out.
tour.story: Giovanni Belzoni found it in 1817. Its alabaster sarcophagus is in a London museum. In 1829 Champollion and the Italian scholar Rosellini cut out wall panels, now in the Louvre and in Florence; one of them shows the goddess Maat with her feather. The tomb shows what the others looked like at their best.

alone.intro: Here I leave you. In the valley the guide cannot follow you inside anyway. Each tomb takes ten to twenty minutes. Do your three general tombs, then decide whether anyone still has the energy for an extra.

plans.d: One tomb close to the entrance, chosen for colour (often Ramesses IX, KV6). Walk slowly down to the burial chamber, find the ceiling, and come back up. Drink in the shade of a shelter before the tram.

Your three general tombs, one long (Ramesses III or Merenptah), one bright (Ramesses IX) and one with graffiti (Ramesses IV). In each: the disc over the door, the hour of the night, the ceiling. Then stop for water.
Do two tombs and go back down on the tram. The tombs are cooler than the valley, but humid and airless deep inside. The visitor centre has shade and seats.

plans.t: If you want one more thing
plans.d: Ramesses VI with the doubled Nut ceiling, then Tutankhamun next to it. Together they tell the story of how one tomb's rubble saved the other.

alone.meet: Meet at the tram stop at the valley entrance at the agreed time. If someone is late, wait in the nearest shelter, not in the sun.

photos.where: On the main path inside the valley, at a point where the peak rises above the slopes behind you.
photos.when: Early morning, when the sun is still low in the east and part of the valley is in shade.
photos.how: Six in a line, peak above the middle of the group. Phone low, slightly upward, so the peak and blue sky fill the top.
photos.avoid: Tomb queues and tour groups behind you, and the sun in your faces.

photos.where: In front of any tomb entrance with a clear sign and number.
photos.when: Mid-morning, when the doorway is lit and the inside is dark.
photos.how: Frame the dark rectangle of the doorway with the rock above it. One person at the top of the steps for scale.
photos.avoid: Guards and the queue in the doorway.

photos.where: Near the steps down to Tutankhamun's tomb, without blocking them.
photos.when: Whenever the queue is short.
photos.how: One person looks into the stairwell holding an imaginary candle, the others crowd behind. Caption: wonderful things.
photos.avoid: Blocking the stairs, stepping over barriers.

photos.where: Burial chamber of KV9 or KV6, if photos are allowed.
photos.when: Any time.
photos.how: 0.5x, phone flat facing straight up from the centre of the room. Hold still, let night mode work.

details.d: The cobra goddess of the peak, 'she who loves silence'. Workmen prayed to her not to be punished with blindness or illness.
In the Book of Gates each gate has a serpent standing on its tail. Count the gates you pass.
In unfinished tombs you can sometimes see red guide lines and draft drawings that the outline draughtsman left.
Corridor ceilings often carry a vulture with wings spread, flying deeper into the tomb with you.
Some tombs have a deep shaft after the first corridors: against floods, against robbers, or a ritual tomb of Osiris. Scholars still debate.
Ancient tourists wrote their names and comments, sometimes complaining that they could not read the hieroglyphs.
Late sarcophagi are shaped like a cartouche, the oval ring round a royal name: the king lies inside his own name.
Look at the slope above Tutankhamun's stairs. The workmen's huts that hid it stood there.
Wooden floors and glass panels were added to stop visitors brushing the walls. Every breath adds humidity inside.
In 2025 a tomb in a side valley about two kilometres west was confirmed as his, the first royal tomb identified since 1922.

qa.q: Which three tombs should we choose?
qa.a: It depends on what is open, so ask your guide on the day. A good family mix is one long, deep tomb for the sense of descent (Ramesses III or Merenptah), one with bright colour and a sky ceiling (Ramesses IX), and one near the entrance with ancient graffiti (Ramesses IV). If you buy one extra, Ramesses VI is often named the most beautiful.

qa.q: Is Tutankhamun's tomb worth the extra ticket?
qa.a: For the story, yes; for the art, less. It is small, and the only painted room is the burial chamber. You will see the king himself in his glass case, the sarcophagus and the baboon wall. If the family already saw the treasures at the Grand Egyptian Museum, standing where Carter stood closes the story. If budget or energy is short, Ramesses VI next door has the better walls.

qa.q: Is Seti I's tomb open?
qa.a: Sometimes. It has been closed for long periods for conservation and, when open, it is on the most expensive ticket of the valley. Ask at the ticket office. If it is open and you can afford it, many Egyptologists call it the best-decorated tomb in Egypt.

qa.q: Why are the tombs so deep?
qa.a: Depth followed the theology and the reign. The tomb mirrored the sun's descent into the underworld, and a long reign meant more time to dig. Merenptah's and Seti I's run well over a hundred metres. Short reigns produced short or unfinished tombs, like Tutankhamun's. Some depth also helped against robbers, without much success.

qa.q: Were all the tombs robbed?
qa.a: Almost all, many in antiquity. Around 1000 BC, in hard times, priests emptied the royal tombs, rewrapped the mummies and hid them in two caches, one in the cliffs near Deir el-Bahari, one in the tomb of Amenhotep II (KV35). That is how we have the mummies of Seti I and Ramesses II. Tutankhamun was robbed twice soon after burial but resealed and then forgotten.

qa.q: Can we see Hatshepsut's tomb?
qa.a: No. KV20 runs about two hundred metres into poor rock and is not open. Her father Thutmose I may have been moved into it. Her mummy, if the 2007 identification is right, is in Cairo. The l06 episode covers the debate.

qa.q: How did the workmen light the tombs?
qa.a: With lamps of oil or fat and wicks, which workmen received in counted rations. Studies of the ceilings found very little soot, so they probably added salt to the fuel to stop smoking. Daylight was reflected in from the entrance with polished surfaces, which is an old suggestion that is hard to prove.

qa.q: Is anything still waiting to be found?
qa.a: Probably. Several kings' tombs and mummies are still missing, Amenhotep I among them, and the 2025 confirmation of Thutmose II's tomb in a side valley shows that discoveries still happen. Claims of hidden rooms behind Tutankhamun's walls were tested by radar in 2015 to 2018, with contradictory results; many specialists now doubt a hidden chamber exists.

practical: Optional: confirm with the representative before the day. It is not in the printed programme.
Allow about 2 to 2.5 h with the tram and three or four tombs.
Go as early as you can. By late morning the valley floor reflects heat from every side.
Bring water, hats, sun cream. Toilets and cold drinks are at the visitor centre.
Buy extra tomb tickets at the ticket office before the tram. Check prices and photo rules there.
Flash is always banned. Phone photos inside may or may not be allowed: ask.
Tomb corridors are steep and humid, with wooden walkways and handrails. Anyone with claustrophobia can stay at the top.
Guards may offer a forbidden photo or a closed room for a tip. Decline politely.
Shoes with grip, no bags you need to put down: there are few places to sit.
The tram has a small separate fee; check on the day.

kids.d: In one tomb, find the sun as a scarab, as a disc and as a ram-headed man. Which one is morning?
In a tomb with the Book of Gates, count the serpents guarding gates. How many hours of night did you pass?
After one tomb, draw its plan from memory: corridors, rooms, the burial chamber. Compare with the model.
Find Greek letters scratched near an entrance. How old is the oldest graffiti you can see?
Should Tutankhamun's mummy stay in his tomb, or join his treasure in the museum? One minute for each side.
Explain why the walls are a map of the night and how the king hoped to rise again with the sun.

glossary.d: Kings' Valley: the tomb numbering, KV1 to about KV65.
'What is in the underworld': the sun's twelve hours of night.
The night divided by twelve gates, each guarded by a serpent.
Sky goddess whose body arches across burial chamber ceilings.
'The horn', the pyramid-shaped peak above the valley.
Cobra goddess of the peak, 'she who loves silence'.
The village of the tomb builders, over the hill.
Son and successor of Ramesses II, tomb KV8.

tonight: Which tomb was your favourite, and what made it different from the others?
If you were designing a tomb for yourself, what would you put on the walls?
The workmen's rubble saved Tutankhamun's tomb. What other lucky accidents saved things in history?

dia-pyramid-evolution.title: A century of trial and error
dia-pyramid-evolution.alt: Side-view silhouettes of seven pyramids to a common scale on two ground lines. Row one: Djoser's Step Pyramid, about 62 m, six steps, c.2670 BC; Meidum, originally about 92 m, now a tower, Sneferu c.2600 BC; Bent Pyramid, about 105 m, slope changing from about 54 to about 43 degrees halfway up; Red Pyramid, about 104 m at about 43 degrees, the first true smooth-sided pyramid. Row two: Khufu's Great Pyramid, originally about 147 m at about 52 degrees, c.2560 BC; Khafre's, about 144 m, on higher ground so it looks taller, c.2530 BC; Menkaure's, about 65 m, lower courses in red granite, c.2510 BC. A tiny person at Khufu's foot shows the scale.

dia-saqqara-route.title: Djoser's Step Pyramid complex
dia-saqqara-route.alt: Plan sketch of Djoser's rectangular enclosure at Saqqara, north up, long side north-south (about 545 by 277 m). Visit order: 1 entrance colonnade in the south-east corner, 2 Great South Court, 3 Step Pyramid, 4 Heb-Sed court with dummy chapels on the east side, 5 serdab with Djoser's statue north-east of the pyramid, 6 South Tomb by the south wall. The wall has 15 gates, 14 false and one real. Inset: the Pyramid of Unas and its causeway to the south-west; the Imhotep Museum by the site entrance.

map-giza.title: The Giza plateau
map-giza.alt: Map of the Giza plateau, north at the top. Three pyramids stand in a diagonal line from north-east to south-west: Khufu (the Great Pyramid, the biggest), Khafre, and Menkaure (the smallest), with small queens' pyramids beside them. The Sphinx sits east of Khafre, near the escarpment edge, with the town of Nazlet el-Samman beyond it. The old solar boat museum site is on the south side of Khufu; the boat moved to the Grand Egyptian Museum, which lies to the north-west, in 2021. The pyramid builders' town (Heit el-Ghurab) is to the south-east, beside the Wall of the Crow.

dia-giza-khufu-section.title: Inside the Great Pyramid
dia-giza-khufu-section.alt: Schematic north-south cross-section of the Great Pyramid of Khufu. The original entrance is on the north face about 17 m above the ground; the Descending Passage runs down into the bedrock to an unfinished underground chamber. The Ascending Passage branches up to the Grand Gallery, which leads to the King's Chamber; a horizontal passage leads to the Queen's Chamber. A dashed shape above the Grand Gallery marks the ScanPyramids Big Void, found in 2017, about 30 m long. Al-Mamun's tunnel, about AD 820, is the break-in route the public uses today. The interior visit is not part of the programme.

dia-nile-seasons.title: The three seasons of the Nile
dia-nile-seasons.alt: Circular calendar of the three ancient Egyptian seasons around a month ring: Akhet, the flood, about July to November, when the river covered the fields and left black mud; Peret, the growing season, about November to March, when farmers sowed and crops grew; Shemu, the harvest, about March to July, when crops were cut and the river was lowest. A note says the Aswan High Dam (1970) ended the yearly flood.

dia-karnak-route.title: Karnak: the main axis, west to east
dia-karnak-route.alt: East-west schematic of the main axis of the Amun precinct at Karnak, north up, the Nile on the west. Numbered stops in the usual order: 1 avenue of ram-headed sphinxes, 2 First Pylon, 3 Great Court with the Kiosk of Taharqa in the middle, the Temple of Seti II to the north and the Temple of Ramesses III to the south, 4 Second Pylon, 5 Great Hypostyle Hall with 134 columns, 6 obelisks between the Fourth and Fifth Pylons including Hatshepsut's, 7 the Sacred Lake and giant scarab south of the axis, 8 the Festival Hall of Thutmose III at the east end. The axis leads from the Nile inland; the walking route is up to the guide.

dia-edfu-route.title: Edfu temple: the visit in 8 stops
dia-edfu-route.alt: Plan of Edfu temple with the entrance at the bottom and the sanctuary at the top, eight numbered stops: 1 granite falcon statues of Horus at the gate, 2 the pylon with the king smiting enemies, 3 the open court with its colonnade, 4 the first hall of columns, 5 the second hall, 6 the offering hall, 7 the sanctuary with the granite shrine, 8 the corridor that runs all round the temple core inside the enclosure wall, with reliefs of Horus against Set. A note says to ask the guide about the calèche drop-off and ticket gate.

dia-temple-section.title: Into the temple, step by step
dia-temple-section.alt: Long section through a typical Egyptian temple, using Edfu as the example, entrance on the left. From left: the pylon and gate; the open sun court under the sky; the first hall of columns; a second, smaller hall; the offering hall; the sanctuary with the god's shrine. The floor steps up and the ceiling steps down towards the sanctuary while the rooms get darker, shown by an arrow from sun and crowd to dark and god.

dia-kom-ombo-plan.title: Kom Ombo: one temple, two gods
dia-kom-ombo-plan.alt: Plan of the double temple of Kom Ombo with north at the top and the Nile on the entrance side. A dashed centre line splits it: the north half belongs to Haroeris (Horus the Elder, falcon-headed, sky and war god), the south half to Sobek (crocodile god of water and fertility). Two entrances lead along two aisles through the halls to two sanctuaries at the back, inside shared outer walls: twin doors, twin halls, twin sanctuaries.

dia-high-dam.title: The Aswan High Dam
dia-high-dam.alt: Simple cross-section of the Aswan High Dam: Lake Nasser behind it to the south (about 500 km long), the embankment dam (about 3.8 km long, 111 m high, built 1960 to 1970) with a power station at its downstream foot, and the Nile below it flowing north. Note: Philae and Abu Simbel were moved because of this lake.

dia-philae-route.title: Philae: the visit in order
dia-philae-route.alt: Linear route of the Philae visit with eight numbered stops: 1 boat from the landing to Agilkia Island, 2 Kiosk of Nectanebo and the west colonnade, 3 First Pylon, 4 court with the Birth House (Mammisi), 5 Second Pylon, 6 hall and sanctuary of Isis, 7 Gate of Hadrian and the Osiris rooms, 8 Trajan's Kiosk by the water as the last view. A ribbon notes that the original Philae island is under the lake and the temples stand on Agilkia, moved in the 1970s.

dia-hatshepsut.title: Hatshepsut's temple: three terraces
dia-hatshepsut.alt: Front elevation of Hatshepsut's temple at Deir el-Bahari against the curved cliff, seen looking west, so south is on the left and north on the right. Three terraces climb towards the cliff, joined by a central ramp. The lower terrace has colonnades with Osiride statues. On the middle terrace, the south end holds the Punt colonnade and the Chapel of Hathor, the north end the Birth colonnade and the Chapel of Anubis. The upper terrace has the sun court and the sanctuary cut into the cliff. Note: the temple copies the bowl of the cliff and faces east across the river towards Karnak.

map-egypt-route.title: Your route through Egypt
map-egypt-route.alt: Map of Egypt with the Nile, the delta, Lake Nasser, the Mediterranean and the Red Sea. The route: fly from Paris to Cairo on day 1, stay in the Cairo area until day 4, fly to Luxor on day 4, cruise up the Nile to Aswan (days 5 to 7) and back to Luxor (days 8 to 10), fly home from Luxor on day 11. A dotted line marks the optional road trip from Aswan to Abu Simbel, about 280 km.

dia-timeline.title: Who built what, and when
dia-timeline.alt: Horizontal timeline from 2700 BC to AD 2026, linear scale with a break between AD 400 and 1900. Period bands: Old Kingdom c.2686-2181 BC, Middle Kingdom c.2055-1650 BC, New Kingdom c.1550-1069 BC, Ptolemaic 305-30 BC, Roman 30 BC-AD 395, then modern. Markers, each tagged with where the family sees it: Djoser c.2670 BC (Saqqara), Khufu c.2560 BC (Giza), Hatshepsut c.1479-1458 BC, Amenhotep III c.1390-1353 BC, Ramesses II c.1279-1213 BC and Ramesses III c.1184-1153 BC (all Luxor), Tutankhamun c.1332-1323 BC (GEM, Cairo), Edfu temple built 237-57 BC, Philae temples Ptolemaic and Roman with the last hieroglyphs AD 394 (Aswan), Tutankhamun's tomb found 1922, Philae moved in the 1970s, Grand Egyptian Museum opened 2025.

map-cairo.title: Cairo and the pyramid fields
map-cairo.alt: Map of the Cairo area with the Nile running north through the city. West of the river: the Grand Egyptian Museum and the Giza pyramids, the hotel area (approximate) further west, and to the south Saqqara, Memphis in the fields, and the Dahshur pyramids. Cairo airport is in the north-east. Straight-line distances: Giza to Saqqara ~14 km, Saqqara to Memphis ~5 km, Saqqara to Dahshur ~7 km.

map-saqqara.title: Saqqara, Memphis and Dahshur
map-saqqara.alt: Map of the Saqqara area, north at the top. The desert plateau on the west holds Abusir in the north, the Step Pyramid of Djoser with the Unas pyramid just south of it, and the Red and Bent pyramids of Dahshur at the bottom. To the east, green fields mark the Nile valley, with Memphis (Mit Rahina museum) among them; the Nile itself is further east. Straight-line distances: Memphis to the Step Pyramid ~5 km, Step Pyramid to the Red Pyramid at Dahshur ~7 km.

map-nile-cruise.title: The Nile cruise, Luxor to Aswan
map-nile-cruise.alt: Strip map of the Nile from Luxor in the north to Aswan in the south, with river distances: Luxor to Esna (lock) ~60 km, Esna to Edfu ~50 km, Edfu to Kom Ombo ~65 km, Kom Ombo to Aswan ~40 km, about 215 km in all. Temple visits on land at Luxor, Edfu, Kom Ombo and Aswan (Philae). Timeline: day 4 board in Luxor; day 5 Luxor sights, sail to Esna, overnight near Edfu; day 6 Edfu temple, sail via Kom Ombo to Aswan; day 7 Aswan, High Dam, Philae, felucca; day 8 sail back via Kom Ombo to Edfu; day 9 via the Esna lock to Luxor; day 10 west bank; day 11 fly home.

map-luxor.title: Luxor, two banks
map-luxor.alt: Map of Luxor with the Nile flowing north between the two banks. East bank, the city of the living: Luxor Temple in town and Karnak to the north, joined by the Avenue of Sphinxes (about 2.7 km), and Luxor airport to the east. West bank, the city of the dead: the Colossi of Memnon and Medinet Habu at the edge of the fields, the Valley of the Queens, the Temple of Hatshepsut under the cliffs, and the Valley of the Kings (grey, not on your programme).

map-aswan.title: Aswan, the dams and Philae
map-aswan.alt: Map of Aswan, north at the top. The Nile flows north past Aswan town and Elephantine Island. South of town, granite rocks and islets of the first cataract, then the Old Dam. Between the two dams lies a reservoir with the Philae temples on Agilkia Island. Further south the Aswan High Dam holds back Lake Nasser. Straight-line distances: Aswan town to the High Dam ~13 km, High Dam to Philae ~6 km. An arrow points south to Abu Simbel, about 280 km by road, optional.

days.plan: Fly Paris to Cairo. Meet the Sakkara Tours representative. Hotel.
Grand Egyptian Museum. Afternoon: Dahshur (replaces Citadel, mosque, souk).
Fly Cairo to Luxor. Board the cruise boat. Free afternoon.
Luxor Temple and Karnak. Sail about 3 h to Esna.
Edfu by carriage. Kom Ombo. Sail to Aswan. Galabeya party.
High Dam, Philae, felucca on the Nile.
Optional Abu Simbel. Sail about 7 h to Edfu via Kom Ombo.
Sail about 4 h to Luxor, through the Esna lock.
West bank: Valley of the Queens, Colossi, Medinet Habu, Hatshepsut.

cairo.title: Cairo and its pyramids
cairo.lead: Three nights near Giza. Everything below is within about 15 km of the pyramids, except the airport.
rows: Grand Egyptian Museum, a short drive from the plateau.
Dahshur: the two pyramids of Sneferu. This is a suggestion that replaces the Citadel, mosque and souk. Confirm with the representative on Day 1.
Memphis, Saqqara, then the Giza plateau. Distances: Giza to Saqqara about 14 km, Saqqara to Memphis about 5 km, Saqqara to Dahshur about 7 km.

nile.title: The Nile cruise
nile.lead: Seven nights on the boat. The river runs north, so you sail upstream to Aswan and drift back down.
rows: Luxor to Esna, Edfu, Kom Ombo and Aswan on the way up. Back down to Edfu, through the Esna lock, to Luxor.
Luxor Temple and Karnak, Edfu, Kom Ombo, High Dam, Philae, then the west bank of Luxor on Day 10.
Sailing hours are for rest, reading and the river. The Nile life page tells you what to look for.

luxor.title: Luxor: two banks
luxor.lead: The east bank is the city of the living: temples of Luxor and Karnak. The west bank is the city of the dead: tombs and mortuary temples.
rows: Luxor Temple and Karnak, joined by the Avenue of Sphinxes, about 2.7 km.
Valley of the Queens, Colossi of Memnon, Medinet Habu and the temple of Hatshepsut.
The Valley of the Kings. Ask the representative whether it fits on Day 10.

godsLede: Gods are drawn with fixed signs. Learn nine and you can read most walls.
godsNote: Set, the god of chaos and storms, has an animal head no zoologist can name. You meet him at Edfu, as the enemy.

rules: Animals and people in a line of text look toward the start of the line.
Kings and gods are big. Enemies and helpers are small.
White for the south, red for the north. Both together means the whole country.
A cartouche holds a king's name. Count how often one repeats.
The looped cross is life. A god holding it to a king's nose is giving him breath.
Green is rebirth, black is fertile soil, red is power and danger, blue and gold are divine.

card.title: The smiting scene
card.text: On pylons, a huge king grabs a bunch of enemies by the hair and raises a mace. It is a symbol of order beating chaos, repeated for 3,000 years. It is not a record of a single battle. Compare two of them on your trip.

nameTricks: There is no plain L: use the mouth sign (r).
C is k or s. V is f. Z is s. X is k and s. O and U are the quail chick.
Vowels are often left out. Write the consonants and add a quail chick or reed if it looks bare.
Signs can be read left to right or right to left. Pick one direction and face the animals into the start.
nameLede: Sound out your name, then pick signs for the sounds. Draw an oval around them, and you have a cartouche.

kit.title: Sun and heat
items: Expect about 28 degrees C in Cairo and the mid 30s in Luxor and Aswan by day. Evenings are cooler, so a light layer helps on the boat deck and on the early Abu Simbel coach.
Hats, sunglasses, sun cream, closed shoes for sand. Shoulders and knees covered is easy and sun smart.
Plan the heavy sights for the morning. Rest on the boat in the middle of the day.

kit.title: Water and food
items: Sealed bottled water only. Check the seal. Use it for teeth too.
Hand gel before meals. Peeled fruit and cooked food are the safe default.
Ask your doctor or pharmacist about a small kit: rehydration salts and your usual medicines.

kit.title: Money (from your programme)
items: Visa on arrival: 53 EUR per person, in cash euros, handled by the representative.
Tips pool: 65 EUR per person, paid on site. Ask the representative whether children are included.
Optional trips are paid locally. Keep small Egyptian pound notes for toilets, helpers and small tips.

kit.title: Phones and photos
items: Download the app and PDF on hotel Wi-Fi before you board. Boat Wi-Fi is paid and common areas only.
No flash in tombs and museums. Ask the guide before using a tripod or drone, both are usually not allowed.
Ask before photographing people. Do not photograph police or military.

kit.title: Respect and common sense
items: 'La, shukran' (no, thank you) said with a smile ends most sales. 'Shukran' is thank you. 'Yalla' is let's go.
Agree any price before a ride, a photo or a favour. A 'gift' usually has a price.
Stay close to the guide at busy sites. Agree a meeting point when you split up.

kit.title: Clocks
items: Egypt runs ahead of France by 1 hour at first, by 2 hours from 25 to 29 October, then 1 hour again. Your phone adjusts, but sailing and wake-up times are local time.

cards.title: Before you leave the boat
items: Passports, tickets and boarding passes in one place.
Chargers, torches and the tip envelopes.
Check the safe, the cabin and the pool deck for forgotten things.
Your flight leaves Luxor late morning. Your representative sets the time.

cards.title: Five questions for the flight home
items: Which room or place made you go quiet?
Which story would you retell at school?
Which thing did the guide say that you doubt?
What would you like to look up?
Where would you go back to first?

cards.title: Souvenir thoughts
cards.text: Cotton, spices, alabaster and hand-woven things are common. Check that papyrus is real by looking for plant fibres. Prices are a conversation, not a sticker.
